speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Comtois (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement concerning the coal mining industry of Cape Breton. Hon. members will recall that during the past year arrangements were made between the governments of Nova Scotia and Canada on the one hand, and the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation on the other, which successfully averted the closing of three Nova Scotia coal mines last winter. At that time it was agreed that to offset losses incurred by the corporation in maintaining these mines in operation, a special subvention of $1 per ton would be paid on coal shipped by the corporation to non-subvention areas from their mines in Nova Scotia between April 1, 1960 and May 31, 1961. The province participated in the cost of this subvention.
During the past year the markets for coal here and everywhere in the world have continued to shrink, and the annual productive capacity of the corporation's various mines is now substantially greater than the possible level of annual sales. In these circumstances, if the special subvention should be allowed to terminate on May 31 and no alternative assistance be provided, the corporation would be obliged to proceed with the scheduled closures this season and many coal miners in the Cape Breton area would be laid off in the space of less than three months.
The government has discussed this difficult situation further with the corporation, the labour union and the government of Nova Scotia in an endeavour to determine the extent of the problem and the steps that might be taken at this time to alleviate it. I am now able to announce that the subvention of $1 per ton, of which 80 cents will be provided by the federal government and 20 cents by the government of Nova Scotia, up to a total sum of $300,000 per annum, will be continued for the period from June 1, 1961 to August 1, 1962, on the express understanding that the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation will provide satisfactory assurance to the governments that this assistance will be used to good advantage in maintaining as much employment as possible in
the mines. Because of the shrinkage of markets the corporation will be obliged to reduce the number of miners on its payroll.
Authority for this continuing subvention is contained in order in council P.C. 1961/762 of May 25, 1961, and the required funds will be provided in the vote of the dominion coal board.
The government of Canada recognizes that subventions do not constitute a complete long term solution to the problem of employment in the Cape Breton area, and that other kinds of measures are also involved. Indeed, nationwide programs such as the vocational training assistance plan and the tax incentive arrangements included in the recent supplementary budget are already available for use in such areas.
The government considered, however, that as miners are displaced from employment with the corporation this season, other special steps should be taken at this time to assist in the provision of alternative employment. Parliament will therefore be asked to provide an amount of $1.5 million which will be set aside for approved projects to provide alternative employment this year in the Cape Breton area. Such projects will be considered on their individual merits, taking into account the degree of participation by the province in each case.
These two measures are being introduced to deal with the specific and immediate situation in the coal mining areas. The government of Canada is continuing to study the long term problems involved and the recommendations on the subject by the royal commission on coal, and further announcements will be made from time to time.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every hon. member as well as the people of the areas concerned will welcome the announcement made this morning by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. However, as the minister indicated, this is an alternative assistance to prevent the immediate closure of the mines involved, and I am sure it will be regarded as just another one of this government's crisis decisions. The house and the country know very well that as early as 1958, at the time of the first major post-war shut-down, this government was warned of the dangers inherent in the situation. At that time we were ridiculed by the government, just as we are at this very moment by some of the members concerned.

Continuation of Coal Subvention

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think I should remind the hon. member for Gloucester that such a statement is made for the information of the house. It is a statement of a factual character on policy that has been adopted, and it is made by leave of the house for its information rather than having it made elsewhere. It is not made to initiate a debate. The practice of comment by a spokesman for each party has been accepted by the house and is well established, but such comment is not to be in the form of debate. As the hon. member was expressing opinions which are quite controversial, I thought I should warn him that it is not in accordance with our practice to debate the statement at this time. There will be ample opportunity to do so. Really all that is permitted is preliminary comment with a reservation of approval if that is the case.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression that as a member of the opposition I had the right to say that this alternative measure announced by the minister this morning will not meet the problems of the coal miners. It will only mean further delay. As we have suggested before in the house, what is really needed is a comprehensive program of scientific and industrial research to find additional uses for coal in order to help to maintain employment. This is certainly not included in the announcement made by the minister this morning.
We are also disappointed that in the announcement the minister did not take care of the situation in the Springhill area, where a number of miners have been out of work since 1958, notwithstanding the representations that have been made to the government in recent weeks by the town council of Springhill.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the measure announced by the minister will only provide temporary relief, and it does not meet the problems of the coal miners of Cape Breton.

Mr. Speaker, the announcement made this morning is in large part a continuation of the situation that has existed for some time involving the payment of a subvention of $1 per ton. I was not able to understand clearly from the minister's statement whether the three coal mines scheduled to be shut down this summer will in fact be shut down or whether operations will be continued but with a very substantial reduction in the number of miners employed. I should like to have that point clarified.
As far as we are concerned, the government has not taken adequate action in this area, particularly because it is an area of very high unemployment where not long ago 18 per

cent of the labour force were out of work. I think what is required here is a guaranteed income to the miners so that if they are displaced from their jobs they will have a substantial income to maintain themselves and their families. The $1.5 million for approved employment projects will be of great benefit, but I suggest that what is required is a comprehensive program to deal with the general unemployment situation in this area, and that by and large the announcement represents merely a continuation of the existing conditions.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) asked the following question:
Is it an offence for a person to refuse to answer certain of the questions contained in the census forms and, if so, what would be the penalty for such a refusal?
In answer I will quote to him section 35 of chapter 257 of the Statistics Act, which deals with offences and penalties connected with the taking of the census. It reads as follows:
35. Every person who, without lawful excuse,
(a) refuses or neglects to answer, or wilfully answers falsely, any question requisite for obtaining any information sought in respect of the objects of this act or any regulation, or pertinent

thereto, that has been asked of him by any person employed in the execution of any duty under this act or any regulation; or
(b) refuses or neglects to furnish any information or to fill in to the best of his knowledge and belief any schedule or form that he has been required to fill in, and to return the same when and as required of him under this act or any regulation, or wilfully gives false information or practises any other deception thereunder;
is, for every such refusal or neglect, or false answer or deception, guilty of an offence and is liable, upon summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding one hundred dollars, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: LAOS-REPORTED DIFFERENCES BETWEEN CO-CHAIRMEN OF GENEVA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members are aware, difficulties have arisen at the Geneva conference on Laos over questions related to the effectiveness of the cease fire in that country.
The position of the Canadian government in this matter is clear. We are doing our utmost to ensure that the commission has both the authority and the means to carry out its task of supervision and control. We are in favour of the commission investigating any serious violation or threat of violation of the cease fire.
To do this the commission must have two things. First, it must have the co-operation of the parties in Laos. Recent reports indicate agreement by the parties there to the establishment of a joint military committee to work with the international commission. We hope this will help to remove some of the difficulties which have existed so far. Second, the commission must have helicopters, airplanes and other physical facilities. It reported its logistical requirements to the co-chairmen on May 22. We hope that the earliest possible agreement will be reached among the governments principally concerned on supplying at least the most urgent of these requirements.
I might add that newspaper speculation that the Geneva conference is on the verge of collapse is in my view not warranted by any major change in the situation either in Laos or at Geneva. There has been some difference of opinion as to what topic would be discussed next, and I understand that the meeting called for yesterday did not take

On clause 2-Punishment for capital murder.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
On clause 2, Mr. Chairman, I must say that even if I voted against the principle of the bill on second reading, I am very receptive to any reasonable reform.
My mind is not set for or against the abolition of capital punishment. I am in favour of realistic reforms of the penal law concerning the death penalty and I sincerely believe that Bill C-92 is a mere compromise which after all, will lead to results which I do not want.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the greatest threat to our society comes first from organized crime. It is, therefore, against that threat that we must not show any weakness. We must see to it that we are efficiently protected against it through this bill.
In the course of my remarks when the bill was introduced, I said that we should break new grounds and liken the case of women to that of a young man under 18. Indeed if this bill provides that any young man under 18 must be exempted from capital murder, and consequently exempted from the death penalty, I fail to see why we should not, following the same line, do the same in the case of women.
I wish to state here very briefly that we cannot liken the case of women to that of the adult male as far as the death penalty is concerned.
Here is the basis of my argument. I have here the report of the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, and I wish to refer you, Mr. Chairman, to section 1,008:
(Text):

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY

May I raise a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I understand the hon. member is now suggesting the bill should provide that women would not be liable to capital punishment. It seems to me this is not relevant to the clause under discussion. I do not know whether it would have been possible, but I do suggest that the only time it might have been possible to make such a suggestion would have been on second reading, when the bill as a whole was being discussed. I am not saying the subject would have been relevant then and it might have been a matter requiring a ruling, but it seems to me the only time this kind of a suggestion might be in order would be during the debate on second reading.
We have concluded the general discussion which is allowed on clause 1 and we are now dealing with the clauses of the bill, at which

time discussion must be strictly relevant to the clause itself. I suggest, therefore, that my hon. friend has not chosen the right time and is not in order in introducing this subject at this stage. I do suggest that, having completed the debate on second reading and the normally wide ranging discussion on the first clause, we should now confine ourselves to a discussion of the clauses of the bill; otherwise any hon. member would be free to introduce any idea he might have with regard to this subject generally. The time for that type of debate is over. I think, in the interests of preserving order, I should make this submission that it is not in order to discuss the question of exempting women from capital punishment.

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
With all due respect to the minister I feel that the position he is taking now is ridiculous. The minister is suggesting that I should have introduced this amendment on second reading. He should know quite well that we were discussing the principle of the bill at that stage, and we are now dealing with clause 2. Clause 2 provides an exception to the general rule in so far as a minor of 18 or under is concerned.
I have an amendment ready, and I am going to lay the foundation for my amendment. I am going to send you a copy of my amendment, Mr. Chairman, as well as the minister. I shall be ready in due time to meet the arguments of the minister. I suggest I am quite in order in presenting a case for the exemption of women from capital punishment at a time when an exemption is already provided in clause 2. I shall be very brief. (Translation):
I was about to read this:
When a death sentence Is pronounced against a woman, she may ask that her execution be delayed on the ground that she is with child.
This simple fact shows that the case of a woman is obviously not the same as that of a man, and that, with regard to capital punishment, we should approach the situation from different angles.
On Thursday, March 4, 1954, during an investigation by the joint committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on capital punishment, the following questions were asked:
According to you, would it be appropriate to impose the death penalty for women?
Have you any general remarks to make with regard to imposing capital punishment for juveniles and women?
That shows that the issue existed at the time of the investigation, and that it was a matter for concern to committee members who gave the question very special consideration.
This is what the then minister of justice, Hon. Mr. Garson, had to say on the subject during the sitting of May 11, 1954:

subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Well, the question of the commutation of the death penalty imposed upon a woman is one which we judge, I think it is fair to say, with more leniency that we would in the case of a man. I think it is also correct to say that in most cases the moral culpability of the crime of murder as committed by a woman as a rule is less than that of a man, speaking generally.
Now, Mr. Chairman, for the last decade or so, there have been, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, only two cases of women being executed, and in each of these cases, if I remember well, those women were only accessory to the crime, and not the main perpetrators.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that we should be realistic. Woman does not constitute the prime menace, and in her case I do not see why imprisonment for life, which is the sentence for non-capital murder, should not be provided as for a young man of under 18.
I said earlier that I proposed to submit an amendment to that section. I trust I will have the support of the hon. member for Scarborough (Mr. McGee).
Under the circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I move that subsection 3 of section 2 of Bill No. C-92 be amended by adding, at line 9, after the words:
3. Notwithstanding subsection (1),-
The following words:
A female person or-

In that connection may I say this, and I shall be quite brief. We considered this matter carefully and were unable to accept the suggestion that has been made from time to time that there should be a provision that women be not liable to capital punishment. In this connection I would point out that it seems to me that when you are making the basic distinction between capital murder and non-capital murder on the basis of the element of deliberation, if such a crime were committed by a woman the capital penalty should be exigible against her just as it is in the case of the same crime committed by a man. Furthermore, the joint parliamentary committee that considered this matter also studied it very carefully and one of their recommendations, as found at page 23 of their report is this: No special provision for women.

I am merely pointing out that our view in this case was shared by the parliamentary committee or that, if you like to put it in that way, in this case we share the view of the parliamentary committee that considered this whole matter for two years. I have a few remarks to make on this clause particularly with relation to subsection 3 of section 206 of the Criminal Code, which excludes a young person from liability to the penalty for capital murder when such person appears to be under the age of 18 at the time he committed the murder. If we turn to chapter 160 of the revised statutes of 1952, an act respecting juvenile delinquents, we find in section 2(1) (a) a definition of the term "child". The definition reads:
"child" means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of sixteen years, or such other age as may be directed in any province pursuant to subsection 2;
If we turn now to subsection 2 we read:
The governor in council may from time to time by proclamation
(a) direct that in any province the expression "child" in this act means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of eighteen years, and any such proclamation may apply either to boys only or to girls only or to both boys and girls, and (b) revoke any direction made with respect to any province by a proclamation under this section, and thereupon the expression "child" in this act in that province means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of sixteen years.
I wonder why we should have a provision in this bill dealing with the Criminal Code stating that the penalty for capital murder shall not be applicable to a child who appears to be under the age of 18 years, when we have on the statute books the Juvenile Delinquents Act according to which a child is defined as a person under the age of 16 years. Should we not apply the same standard to this section 206 of the Criminal Code dealing with capital murder?
Since I indicated on second reading last Wednesday that I am of the opinion that any person 18 years or over is old enough to take responsibility for committing a capital murder and old enough to be liable for the punishment set for capital murder, I draw the attention of the minister to the possibility of amending this clause of the bill now under consideration so as to amend subsection 3 of section 206, which is clause 2 of Bill No. C-92. Accordingly I move, seconded by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-De-lanaudiere:
That clause 2 be amended by substituting the world "sixteen" for the word "eighteen" in paragraph (3) of section 206.

I only know that in our country we have this problem of juvenile delinquency. It may be that we should take it more seriously and say that our young people should be discouraged from taking part in the gang wars and fights of which we hear so much in the big cities of Canada, in Toronto, Winnipeg, Montreal and even here in Ottawa. My proposed amendment arises from the fact that in most provinces of Canada our young people after they reach the age of 16 are very often independent of their parents. Many of them leave home to work in the cities and separate themselves from the authority of their parents. It may be that we should consider the advisability of amending the act in such a way as to reduce the age limit from 18 to 16.
Moreover, if the hon. member had listened carefully he would remember that I quoted chapter 160 of the revised statutes dealing with juvenile delinquents and tried to establish that since that act defines a child as a person under the age of 16, we should apply the same standard all the way through in the Criminal Code except in matters other than in capital crimes where a province has decided to take advantage of section 2, subsection (2) (a) to increase the age from 16 to 18.
Let us not forget, however, that subsection (2) (b) of the same act gives power to the federal government to revoke any such proclamation. My contention is that taking into account that we have extensive juvenile delinquency in this country, we should consider reducing the age from 18 years to 16 years under clause 2 of the bill now being considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
Perhaps I should say a word at this point, because the question as to what is done in other jurisdictions is of interest

Criminal Code
and the answer might be helpful to the committee. The Gowers commission points out in paragraph 183 that with respect to the United Kingdom the children's act of 1908 provided that persons under 16 years of age at the time of the offence could not be sentenced to death but, instead, could be sentenced to be detained during His Majesty's pleasure. This provision was extended by the children and young person's act of 1933 and by the children and young person's (Scotland) act of 1937 to persons under 18 at the time of conviction. It was further extended by section 16 of the criminal justice act, 1948 and section 17 of the criminal justice (Scotland) act, 1949, to persons under 18 at the time the offence was committed. No person under 18 years of age had in fact been executed since 1887. So the law of England since 1933 has been that no one under the age of 18, generally speaking, should be hanged.
It seems to me, with respect to the argument of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville, that there is some difficulty. He is basing his case on the fact that in our Juvenile Delinquents Act the age limit is stated to be 16, and I believe that is subject to variation from province to province. Assuming that it is age 16, for the purposes of his argument, it seems to me there is a very great difference between saying, on the one hand, that for the purposes of that act a person under the age 16 shall be regarded as a juvenile and shall be treated in special courts, and saying on the other hand that a person over 16 and under 18 years of age, therefore, should be subject to be hanged. One argument does not seem to follow from the other at all.
I should again like to refer to the findings of the joint parliamentary committee here in Canada, and perhaps I should read the whole paragraph from their report in this regard. The paragraph in question is No. 76, found at page 18 of that report, and reads as follows:
76. The committee noticed that the invariable practice has been to commute the sentence of all persons under 18 and that, since 1945, the sentence has rarely been executed against a person 20 years and under. The committee balanced the consideration, that youth must always be a mitigating factor, against the fact that some of the most callous crimes are committed by young offenders showing a total disrespect for life or property. The committee noted that the United Kingdom royal commission on capital punishment unanimously favoured the retention of the present United Kingdom law prohibiting the execution of offenders under 18 but was almost equally divided in considering whether the exemption should be raised to 21. The committee concluded that it would be proper to amend the law to provide that the death penalty should not apply to a person of the age of 18 years or less at the time of the commission of the offence and recommends strongly that, except in extraordinary cases, the present practice of commuting most death sentences passed on persons under 21 years be continued.

This is another case where we have accepted the committee's recommendation, in so far as the provision of the law is concerned, with regard to persons of less than 18 years of age, and it constitutes a recommendation for the guidance of the executive. That viewpoint of the committee is carried into their conclusions or summary of recommendations, and is recommendation No. 6 at page 23.
I recognize that we have to fix an age limit, and that there is bound to be some difficulty because there is a great differentiation made on the basis of perhaps one or two days in a person's life. The limit has to be fixed somewhere, and for the reasons indicated in the passage I have read from the committee's report it seemed appropriate to us that it should be at age 18.

I rather appreciated the sequitur which the minister presented regarding the inconsistencies between the age limit of the Juvenile Delinquents Act and the proposed age limit of 18. That is a very logical approach to the situation. By setting up different age groups in respect of which crimes can be recognized, such as seven years, 14 years, 16 years, and now 18 years, we are
Criminal Code
compounding a great number of difficulties which the different age limitations have created.
As a result, I am wondering how we will deal with the question of the maturity of persons in Canada, when individuals are not considered to be mature for the purpose of voting until the age of 21 years. I suggest that if there is to be a change in respect of the age when a person can be put to death, individuals should be given the full run of their immaturity, so to speak, until they reach the age of 21 years.
Actually we are confusing two things. We are confusing the possibility of finding a person guilty of murder up to a certain age with the advisability of putting that person to death. It is possible to find a person below the age of 16 guilty of murder, but the minister is now asking that he should not be put to death if he is under the age of 18. Therefore I would not support the amendment as it is presented, but on the other hand I would certainly support an amendment to raise the age to 21, to give the Canadian his full run of immaturity until the time he is permitted to vote.

May I draw the committee's attention to what took place in England before the Gowers commission. Paragraph 189 of the report reads:
The statutory exemption of persons under 18 from the capital sentence gave effect to a principle which had governed for over 40 years the practice of ministers responsible for advising on the use of the prerogative of mercy. From 1887 onwards, successive ministers recognized that the penalty of death ought not to be inflicted on persons under the age of 18, and recommended a reprieve in all such cases. The principle that a person under the age of 18 should not be put to death, however bad his crime may be, has long been accepted without question.
In the face of the experience in the United Kingdom and in Canada I think the clause should stand.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, do we not feel that we are giving enough of a chance to these poor people, as we say, who have committed murder? Yesterday, the Prime Minister was saying that, as far as a second offence is concerned, the percentage among criminals having committed murder is less than among other groups of criminals.
That seems normal, because those who have committed homicide are either hanged, which makes for a lower percentage of second offences or they have been imprisoned for life and this again helps to reduce the percentage. The third major group is the one consisting of those who have committed manslaughter; in most cases a car accident is involved and it cannot be said that they are criminals.

Criminal Code
These people, once back to normal life, are not ready to commit new crimes, since they are good people to whom an accident has happened.
As for those who were fortunate enough to be granted mercy and were later released on parole, well they had been sentenced to life imprisonment. If they relapse into crime, they are in for another period of 25 years.
The compassion for those poor murderers expressed by the Prime Minister proceeded from a rather weak argument, I think.
A person of 14 years of age cannot be sentenced to death under the present law. The bill has increased this age level to 18 years. That is why I support the amendment submitted by the member for Chambly-Rou-ville (Mr. Johnson). It keeps closer to the present law, notwithstanding the fact that the bill under discussion gives so many chances to the murderer that it becomes practically impossible to apply the death sentence.
First of all, there is the difference established between capital and non-capital murder.
Yesterday, several examples were given of cases where murderers could not be sentenced to hanging.
Moreover, section 13 of the bill provides that the judge must ask the jury whether or not they recommend mercy for the accused. Under section 14, the judge can also recommend mercy. Section 11 gives the accused an automatic right of appeal the moment the death sentence is passed. Moreover, if he has not been successful before the appeal court, he may, under section 12, bring his case before the supreme court. Finally, if he does not succeed before the supreme court either, there is still the royal prerogative. You know the extent to which that perogative has been used during the past three years; if I am not mistaken, 39 death sentences out of 49 have been commuted to life imprisonment.
I therefore submit, Mr. Chairman, that the murderer has enough chances of avoiding the gallows without our having to set an age limit under which no man may be sentenced to death.
If the government want to abolish capital punishment, why do they not go ahead and say so instead of making a fuss and telling the people in one breath that capital punishment will be abolished and then, in another, that it will not be abolished; that they are in favour of protecting the murderer or that the latter does not have enough protection.
Never have I seen such a misleading and foggy bill aiming to please both currents of opinion. That is why I respectfully submit

that we should support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson).

Mr. Chairman, we are indeed justified in discussing legislation to increase farm income, because the booklet published by the department, entitled "ARDA", reports that out of 575,000 farms operating throughout the country, 120,242 yield only $1,200 or less

Those figures prove what I have said previously to the effect that in the maritime provinces two farmers out of every three do not have enough income to support their family decently. That is why we, in the opposition, have felt it desirable to speak up on behalf of eastern farmers.
Frequently, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) comes back with the charge that we want to pit the eastern farmer against the western farmer. I am not laying the whole blame on the minister for the deplorable situation in which the eastern farmers find themselves, because he is not yet fully conversant with the problems of his department.
It is hard to bring back to earth a man who has been living in the clouds ever since he left his lecturing job at the University of Saskatchewan. However, his irresponsibility would soon be forgiven if we could find among his colleagues in the government, and particularly those from eastern Canada, men with backbone who could truly represent the opinion of eastern farmers.
And what have we heard from the few Quebec members on the government side who have taken part in this debate? Western farmers remember that in 1935 they were in a sorry plight because of successive droughts which had caused large scale social and economic problems. Marginal Lands Development
Out of the 120,000 farms in the eastern provinces, 91,000 do not yield an income of more than $1,200. Is it by planting Christmas trees in the province of Quebec and in other eastern provinces that the Minister of Agriculture intends to provide an answer to the problem of agriculture?
Any attempt to have farmers believe this nonsense is mere window dressing. The problem is in the soil, in the fields, in the barn of the farmer, and not up there in the clouds.

I know two young farmers, in the eastern townships area, who bought a 250 acre farm on which the former owner could barely eke out a living. Today, after about 15 years of operation, the farm has 75 head of cattle and the owners are happy and thriving. These young farmers loved the land, more so, 1 am sure, than people who are quitting the farm in eastern Canada.
There are in eastern Canada a certain number of farms and hundreds of acres of tillable land out of which the owners could make a profit if they were given the means to develop them.
There are certain responsibilities which the government must assume when it is a matter of protecting a whole category of citizens on the way to ruin. This assistance should have as its first objective, the draining of land; second, clearing the land of stones, if necessary; and finally, the fertilizing of grazing land; and crop rotation on tillable lands, and the reforestation on others. Therein lies the whole problem of marginal and submarginal farms in eastern Canada.
I realize that this situation and those difficulties that are met with in eastern Canada are not found out west. I know, having lived and worked on western farms for a year, that they do not have any drainage problem.
They don't have to worry about the problem of the clearing of stones that we have in eastern Canada. Drainage and clearing of stones are two serious disadvantages that we


have to contend with. That is why I would ask that, in this new bill and in the drafting of regulations that will follow, the Minister of Agriculture give special attention to drainage and clearing of stones in eastern Canada.
Years ago, this house enacted the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and all of us have felt its beneficial results. Besides, they are outlined in the publication issued by the Minister of Agriculture. Legislation that would give special attention to drainage and to the clearing of stones would have the same results in eastern Canada as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has had in western Canada.
Of course it would cost several million dollars to apply such a scheme; but would it not be worth while spending a hundred million a year, considering that such a program would benefit six eastern provinces and would help to keep on the land some of the 91,000 farmers who, otherwise, will swell the ranks of the unemployed in the cities?
We are spending about $1,600,000,000 on national defence, to build planes and appliances of war which are obsolete even before they are put into service. Would it not be worth while to sacrifice one or two of these to the cause of agriculture, and to safeguard family farms?
I could go on speaking on this subject, Mr. Chairman, but I shall close my remarks at this point.
However, I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to the request we have placed before him on behalf of eastern farmers. And I urge fellow members from eastern Canada, if the idea I have just put forward is agreeable to them, to give it their support.

At this moment, I should be attending a meeting of the steering committee of the committee on agriculture and colonization. Would it not be possible to arrange the program in such a way that we might attend the proceedings of the house when it is dealing with matters of interest to us, and also attend the meetings of the committee on agriculture and colonization, of whose steering committee I am a member, when it is sitting.

The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska has just indicated that he is a member of the steering committee of a committee of this house dealing with agriculture, and if I understood him aright, he wondered why this matter could not be allowed to stand so he could discharge his responsibilities there. The minister

did not make any physical move that would indicate his interest in the suggestion made by the hon. member. While he is thinking about the request made by the hon. gentleman, I should like to make a few remarks on this particular clause.
Clause 3 (1) (a) provides as follows:
3. (1) The minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, enter into an agreement with any province providing for
(a) the undertaking jointly with the government of the province or any agency thereof of projects for the development of income and employment opportunities in rural agricultural areas specified in the agreement and for improving standards of living in those areas;
With regard to subclause (a) I have this comment to make. Of course no one in this chamber will fail to support any positive effort by the administration for the purpose of promoting projects that will develop income and employment opportunities in rural or other areas in our country; nor will any hon. member oppose any efforts made by the administration to improve the standard of living in those areas. I make these observations because of what I am now going to say, and I hope the minister will not suggest that my remarks now can be construed as meaning that we are not interested in seeing an improvement in the standard of living of the farmers of our country or that we are not anxious to see an improvement in their income and their employment opportunities.
However, I suggest to the minister that this kind of language in a bill is most unusual. The purposes or the objectives of a bill are generally stated in the preamble, and in the preamble of this bill the objectives of this legislation are stated, and I believe they are stated accurately, although I repeat that the bill is no more than a long term measure and does not in any way provide for any immediate improvement in agricultural economic conditions. To use the language in the first clause of the preamble, "their standard of living". The use of the phrases "development of income and employment opportunities" and "improving standards of living" in subclause (a) of clause 3 is a misuse of the form of legislative enactment traditionally resorted to in the House of Commons. The only purpose I can conceive for the inclusion of those phrases in this particular clause is in keeping with the general objective for which this minister in particular is especially noted, namely for propaganda purposes.
The clause itself does nothing to promote income and employment opportunities, nor does it do anything to improve standards of living. It simply gives the government, if it wishes to act, the authority to enter into
Marginal Lands Development agreements with the provinces for the promotion of projects which may have those objectives. But I say that, the objectives having been stated in the preamble, to repeat them in this way in the clause clearly reveals the immediate purpose the administration has in mind, notwithstanding whatever denial may come from the minister.
As I said before, I hope the minister will not misconstrue what I have said. Any project that will improve income and employment opportunities of the farmers in this country will be supported by every member of this committee. Any measure that will improve the standards of living of farmers will be supported by all members of this committee. But if one takes those phrases out of this clause practically nothing remains, and all that we in this committee are asked to vote on with regard to this clause is something that is already covered in the preamble, and is so general as to warrant the indictment I have made about the use of these phrases in an enactment that is supposed to create a new power for the administration pursuant to an act of parliament.

The payment to the province of contributions in respect of the cost of such projects undertaken by the government of the province or any agency thereof.
Can the minister tell us whether it is the intention of the government of Canada, before prorogation, to bring forward by way of a supply estimate any proposed expenditure that might embrace this particular subclause

Marginal Lands Development concerning the payment of contributions to a province? If the minister has a particular project in mind; if he anticipates, as he indicated when we discussed this matter on second reading that he will have at least a pilot project operating in each of the provinces, then it ought to be possible for him to say that it is his intention to bring forward a supplementary estimate providing for an amount of money to cover the payment to the provinces of contributions in respect of particular projects or pilot projects.

While I am dealing with clause 3(l)(b) I might say to the minister that I doubt very much whether the words "or any agency thereof" fully meet the question put by the hon. member for Assiniboia the other day and the reply thereto by the Minister of Agriculture. The hon. member for Assiniboia wanted to know whether this bill would authorize the minister to enter into any arrangements with individual farmers or proprietors, and the minister replied, as I recall, that the bill would authorize the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces so as to enable arrangements to be made with certain delegated bodies which might be composed of groups of farmers or landowners.
Assuming that this was the reply given by the minister, and I believe it was, is the minister satisfied that the words "or any agency thereof" give him the desired kind of authority? Surely this phrase means precisely what it says, an agency of the province. It might be a research board, it might be a farm loan board, it might be a marketing board or some body of that sort, but surely an agency of the province, unless there is a more precise definition, does not mean anybody to whom the province delegates a particular function under the authority which is alleged to exist in this bill. If the minister wants to do that very thing- and I believe he should want to do it-there


ought to be more precise language in this statute so it may be clear that we are authorizing the government to enter into arrangements with the provinces to provide for the delegation to non-governmental bodies of responsibility for carrying out the purposes of this bill.
The comment I made about the use in a legislative enactment of a certain form of words with respect to clause 3(l)(a) as distinguished from a preamble apply equally, of course, to clause 3(2), which says:
For the purpose of assisting the development of income and employment opportunities in rural agricultural areas in Canada and the improvement of standards of living in those areas, the minister may cause to be prepared and undertaken with the government of any province or any agency thereof or with any university, educational institution or person, programs of research and investigation, and co-ordinate such programs with other similar programs being undertaken in Canada.
That is a very laudable objective. Once again, of course, it is an objective addressed to the long term and not designed to bring any immediate redress to the farm income situation. But why is it necessary to restate, as the minister does in the first two lines of this subclause, lines 28 and 29 of this bill, the words "for the purpose of assisting the development of income and employment opportunities in rural agricultural areas in Canada"?
Of course that is the purpose. But the place to state it, as we all know, is in the preamble of the bill, and there it is already stated. To repeat it, as is done here, in the body of the bill is to prostitute the form of legislative enactment which is designed to state the law precisely without giving the author of the measure an opportunity of parading intentions which are, in any case, already stated in the preamble to the bill. It is not necessary to pass this preamble at all if this particular language is going to appear in this clause as it does in some other clauses of the bill.
I suggest to the minister that this draftsmanship is not in accordance with our practice in this house. It is bad draftsmanship. It is draftsmanship of a kind which I am sure was not initiated by the officials of the Department of Justice.
Moreover, I regret that this clause, important as it may be for the future, does not give any relief whatsoever to the farmers of Canada at the present time. That is a fact, notwithstanding all the minister has said in this house, notwithstanding what he has said in the speeches he has made throughout the country, notwithstanding all he has said in the pamphlet which has been printed in hundreds of thousands and copies of which have gone out from one end of this country

to another as representing an accomplished fact when this is nothing more than an intention; an intention to be realized in the distant future; an intention, moreover, which was born not in the mind of the Minister of Agriculture but in the mind of a former prime minister of this country who caused a study to be made of the whole question of rehabilitation, conservation and land use. I refer to Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monleith (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-99, to amend the Food and Drugs Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the measure in respect of which it is my privilege to move second reading is one that I am sure will be of considerable interest to the house. Hon. members are aware of the publicity which has been directed to what are referred to in the criminal underworld vernacular as goof balls. While there is no legal definition for this term, it is widely used to describe a barbiturate or an amphetamine tablet when employed for a non-medical purpose. Goof balls are frequently combined with an alcoholic beverage and are deliberately taken to provide a kick or stimulus which the user either requires or finds enjoyable.
I am advised that these substances are sometimes used by criminals to give them a feeling of confidence or courage in their commission of crime. Another use of these substances involves young people and here the practice is particularly vicious. Teenagers frequenting dance halls and other places of amusement or entertainment, will employ goof balls as a chemical crutch to get some form of stimulus, lift or kick, as the case may be. In addition, narcotic addicts when deprived of narcotics will often turn to these substances for help or support until narcotic medication becomes available. Alcoholics may also use them in a similar manner.
Barbiturates when used for medical purposes are regarded as sedatives and are principally employed for sleeplessness and for the relief of emotional stress or strain.

Food and Drugs Act
Under medical supervision, they are extremely beneficial and are widely used. When improperly used tor the purposes I have indicated, they are not only harmful but frequently disastrous, if not tragic, in their results. They are habit forming if continually or indiscriminately used and in some respects can be said to be addictive.
Amphetamines, under medical supervision, are employed for a number of purposes. They are essentially used for appetite control to reduce overweight, and to relieve mental depression. Because of their stimulating effect on the nervous system, they are capable of helping to sustain mental or physical effort. They combat drowsiness and impede sleep. I am advised that they are often employed by persons engaged in more or less monotonous occupations requiring long hours of effort. Truck drivers on long hauls are frequently reported to use amphetamines to keep them awake and alert.
Experience has shown that persons using amphetamines may require barbiturates to counteract their effect and, conversely, persons using barbiturates may require amphetamines for the same purpose. Their association in the case of motor vehicle operators can be particularly hazardous.
Several years ago, reports were received indicating that barbiturates and amphetamines were easily procurable without a prescription in a number of retail pharmacy outlets. It was not considered, however, that there existed any form of illicit underworld traffic in these substances.
Investigations were subsequently made by inspectors of the food and drug directorate in an attempt to ascertain the extent to which these drugs could be purchased without a prescription in retail stores. As a result of a survey made some four years ago of 2,400 drug stores-or approximately half the total number in Canada-evidence was secured which warranted prosecutions being instituted against some 150 pharmacists. This evidence, however, did not indicate any widespread illicit traffic in these drugs but rather infractions of the requirements of the regulations calling for the sale only upon a prescription.
Within the past year and a half or so, however, other reports have reached us indicating that apart from some infractions of the regulations by retail pharmacists, there also existed a form of illicit underworld traffic in these drugs. This has been investigated by the R.C.M.P. and the results of their investigation clearly support the present existence of such a traffic.

I thought it would be useful if I reviewed very briefly the development of this situation, including the steps that have been taken under the present legislation, as well as the necessity for the additional measures which are now up for consideration.
The hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque), who has discussed this matter on previous occasions in the house, will, I am sure, be glad to know that the government has been fully conscious of the situation and has for some time had under consideration possible ways by which the problem could be effectively met.
While from information gathered by the R.C.M.P. it is clear that a traffic in goof balls does exist in the major cities where there is a criminal underworld element, the situation in Montreal was considered sufficiently serious by the mayor of that city to convene a citizens' committee to deal with the problem. The committee, consisting of all interested groups and organizations, has issued a report recommending that certain steps be taken to combat it. I am pleased to inform the house that our original thinking in developing the measure which is now under consideration, included the very steps which the committee has subsequently recommended for adoption.
In view of the existence of an illicit traffic in barbiturates and amphetamines, hon. members may well wonder why it would not be simpler or preferable merely to include them with narcotics and to deal with the traffic as part of the narcotic traffic. The question is particularly relevant inasmuch as the measures which are proposed to deal with the illicit traffic in these substances are comparable in some respects with the measures which are necessary for the narcotic traffic. There are, however, differences which make it desirable that despite the similarity of enforcement measures, they should be dealt with under separate pieces of legislation.
In the first place, goof balls cannot be classed as narcotics. They are not so classed by the international agencies. Secondly, their medical use is different from that of narcotics. They are much more commonly employed by practitioners than are narcotics. Any proposal, therefore, to deal with barbiturates and amphetamines as narcotics would not receive favour or support from the medical profession. Their objection to such a course would be heightened by the additional psychological reason that it would be unfortunate to characterize barbiturates and amphetamines as narcotics and thus give them the form of stigma that is ordinarily associated with any continued need for, or use of, narcotics.

There is one further difference which of itself requires that barbiturates and amphetamines should be dealt with for legal purposes under the Food and Drugs Act and not as narcotics under that legislation. I refer to the question of possession.
Both in the narcotic act, as well as in this bill, there is established the offence of trafficking and of possession for the purpose of trafficking. Trafficking is the illegal distribution of drugs and it follows that possession for that purpose is related to trafficking but with some procedural difference in its proof. It goes without saying that in the case of a charge of possession for the purpose of trafficking, an important element would be the quantity found and the circumstances under which it was found. This has been substantially the criterion in narcotic enforcement and would be similarly applied in the case of an offence under the proposed Food and Drugs Act amendment.
In the case, however, of simple possession and not possession for the purpose of trafficking, there will be an important difference between narcotic legislation and that contained in this bill. The possession of a narcotic in any form other than as provided in the act or the regulations is a punishable offence. It is not proposed except in the case of possession for trafficking to make such possession a punishable offence under the Food and Drugs Act.
The reason for this difference is the clear distinction that can be drawn between narcotics and the drugs covered by this bill. Narcotics are not normally drugs which would be kept in the home, whereas barbiturates, and to some extent amphetamines, are quite likely to be included in the family medicine cabinet.
Narcotics as a rule would be prescribed on a very limited basis and for a particular purpose which would generally preclude any quantity or supply being on hand after the immediate need had disappeared. This, however, is not the case with barbiturates and in many households in Canada it is customary to maintain a supply of barbiturates for sleeplessness or for use by way of harmless sedation. Although these drugs can be obtained only pursuant to a prescription, which in turn is directed to a particular member of the family, they may be and frequently are used by other members of the family who are not covered by the prescription. It is not considered necessary or desirable that the use of a barbiturate by a member of the family under these circumstances should be made a crime. For this reason, the legislation does not, except as 90205-6-353i
Food and Drugs Act
regards possession for the purpose of trafficking, make simple possession-even when not supported by legal authority-a criminal offence.
Family use under these circumstances is not the evil at which the legislation is aimed and this of itself would require a difference in the enforcement approach.
In addition to the above reasons, it is not thought necessary or desirable that the present illicit traffic in barbiturates and amphetamines should be dramatized or given the importance of the illicit traffic in narcotics and it follows that lesser penalties are considered to be sufficient under the circumstances.
I trust that this explanation will suffice to assure hon. members that this aspect has been given very careful consideration and that despite the similarity of the enforcement aspects, there is good reason for the separation. This, however, will not result in any duplication of effort or of enforcement because the R.C.M.P. will handle the illicit traffic in goof balls along with the illicit traffic in narcotics.
Apart from the suppression of the illicit traffic which will be a responsibility of the R.C.M.P. and, where necessary, other local enforcement agencies, the legal importation and distribution of these substances will be subjected to stricter control than is considered necessary in the case of other drugs which are subject to the Food and Drugs Act.
At the present time, the drugs covered by this bill can be sold only on a prescription and it is not proposed that this will be changed in any way. We do feel, however, that stricter control at the importation, manufacturing and distribution levels is required. This in no sense will impede or interfere with the legal availability of these drugs for proper medical purposes.
Unfortunately, the sources from which traffickers obtain their supplies of goof balls are not always ascertainable. It may be that they are sometimes obtained by theft or diversion from legal sources or it may be that in some cases they are illicitly manufactured. It is felt, however, that if legal sources are substantially tightened, then to the extent that goof balls are obtained by diversion, that source of supply will of itself disappear.
The tightening up of control, therefore, really involves the licensing of importers, manufacturers and wholesale distributors as well as the keeping of special records by such persons which will be subject to audit and examination. This will enable the tracing of supplies to the point of retail distribution in the course of which any unusual or improper dealings will automatically come to light.

Food and Drugs Act
None of these requirements will, however, impose any undue burden on those legitimately engaged in or dealing with these substances and I can assure hon. members that from discussions with the industry no difficulty is expected in bringing about full compliance with the new controls that are proposed.
Respecting the legal medical use of these drugs, there have been reports from time to time indicating dangers from a growing use of or dependence on them. The evidence which is available does not substantiate to any extent the fears so expressed. However, there is no question that in modern society a growing dependence is developing on certain chemical substances for stress, strain and other matters which perhaps were unknown to our forefathers in more leisurely times.
The legislation does not purport to interfere with the legitimate use of any drugs but merely attempts to provide such controls as may be necessary to ensure that proper safeguards accompany the manufacture, distribution and use of drugs where necessary.
The possibility of loose or indiscriminate prescribing of controlled drugs by a very few medical practitioners in Canada will be effectively met by the new measures which are proposed. I am glad, moreover, to assure the house that these proposals have in principle been discussed with representatives of organized medicine who are in agreement with their purpose.
I should like to say at this point that while authority will be provided in the law requiring the keeping of special records by all persons who deal in these substances-and this could well include members of the professions-there is no present intention that practitioners will be required to keep any special records in addition to those which are normally involved in good medical practice. Retail pharmacists will be required to keep special records but these will not be other than those normally required in good pharmaceutical practice. At the same time, authority will be included in the regulations to require a particular individual to furnish explanation as may be necessary respecting his use of these substances and to provide for such information, if necessary, being furnished to the provincial licensing authorities responsible for his right to practise.
I have attempted to set forth the problem in as factual and objective a way as possible so that hon. members will understand its extent and the necessity for the measures which are proposed for its solution. We have every reason to believe that the problem will be effectively checked by these proposals. We are convinced, however, that unless adequate

measures are taken, the problem could well grow in size and importance and become increasingly difficult to remedy.
I can assure the house that the proposals which are set out in this measure are those which in the opinion of the competent authorities-including the R.C.M.P., officers of my department and others who are familiar with the problem-will be adequate and effective. It is our view that every measure needed to stamp out the illicit traffic should be taken and the legislation is designed to permit this being done. At the same time, it is not thought necessary or desirable that any undue restrictions should be placed on the legitimate employment of controlled drugs for medical purposes and the legislation will not have such an effect. Rather, it is the hope of the government that the proposed amendment will bring the matter under control so that it may never reach the proportions of the problem posed by narcotics.
In conclusion, it may be appropriate to mention that the problem which I have described as existing in Canada with regard to barbiturates and amphetamines is also one that is to be found in other countries. I am advised that many other countries at the present time are giving serious consideration to what effective measures should be taken to control the dangers resulting from the unnecessary and non-medical use of these very substances. It is, I think, fitting that Canada should be among the first nations to recognize the problem and to take appropriate action to deal with it.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that, after all these years, the government has at last realized that there is such a thing as a goof ball problem. I hope that now when I speak of the goof ball problem hon. members will realize that it is a serious one, as is now recognized by the government. At the time when I first spoke about goof balls there were perhaps two or three hundred goof ball addicts, but unfortunately the number has grown to such an extent that I think the government is going to have a difficult time attempting to control these drugs.
At the present time these drugs can be obtained in Montreal proper. I know that because I come from Montreal. They can be obtained there in capsules. Some capsules are pink and others are of various colours. The capsules are small in size, being about half an inch in length and about one eighth of an inch in diameter. I presume that these capsules are prepared by the pushers or peddlers of the drugs. They are easily obtainable, I understand.

Hon. members may recall that last week I displayed some 1,500 or 1,800 different clippings which I have gathered over the last few years from various newspapers. They included editorials and full page articles in the weekly papers. In particular they illustrated the danger of the goof ball problem in Montreal. Hundreds of youths have been driven to crime through the use of these drugs and those hon. members who read newspaper articles on this subject only a short time ago will know that crimes have been committed in Montreal which are directly attributable to the use of goof balls, including riots in penitentiaries. One young man went into a cabaret at night and asked to be served with liquor. The bartender said he could not be served. The young man went home, got a revolver, took a goof ball and returned to the club. He waited at the door from midnight to four o'clock and when the bartender came out at four o'clock he shot his head off.
A young man or a young woman who is given goof balls will stop at nothing. Persons so affected will commit any crime, because they lose control and become completely crazy. They have no control over their senses. I am glad the government has at last realized that this is a serious problem and that measures should be taken to include this drug within the provisions of the Food and Drugs Act and allow the R.C.M.P. to handle these cases, because it is not for an amateur to handle this problem.
I wonder whether the minister has received a delegation which was formed in Montreal lately. I notice that the mayor of Montreal has written to the minister. He had arranged for meetings to be held in Montreal of a group of people including police authorities, prominent drug authorities, scientists, college professors and others who realize the danger which is caused to any city when drugs such as these can be obtained by anyone who wants to buy them. I repeat that I am indeed glad that the minister has seen fit to take up this question. Perhaps it will not be possible now to eradicate the practice of resorting to these barbiturates, but I hope the R.C.M.P. will have a better control over the situation and be placed in a better position to see that our youth is not contaminated further by pushers who will stop at nothing to put them in the way of crime.

With respect to the bill before us, it does indicate, I think, that the government realizes that this is a serious problem. I know that it has been so, and increasingly so, in the city of Vancouver for a few years. Vancouver, of course, has the highest population of narcotics addicts
Food and Drugs Act
in Canada and it would possess along with that, a similar interest in barbiturates as they are generally called.
I was reading the Vancouver Sun yesterday, and if I can make a brief reference to the issue of May 27, 1961 with respect to this matter I would mention an article by a Vancouver Sun reporter who visited certain places in Vancouver, bars, restaurants and the like, and purchased from people there a number of goof balls or what he identified as seconal capsules for 50 cents each. I do not want to refer to the article by reading sections from it. Generally, what he discovered was that these barbiturates were being sold somewhat secretively in the places he visited, and there was a continual reference to the need to be more secretive about it because the law was getting more tough in ferreting out those behind this trade in barbiturates or so called good balls. During the course of three hours this reporter bought 11 seconal tablets or capsules for 50 cents each from various persons. All he had to do was to make inquiries of a waiter or someone in a cafe or of some of the people who lounge around the streets in some parts of Vancouver and he had no difficulty in purchasing 11 of these tablets or vials within a period of three hours.
I think one of the reasons why there has been a larger traffic in barbiturates in Vancouver than in other parts of Canada is because of the high proportion of narcotics addicts on the west coast. Narcotics addicts sometimes use certain types of barbiturates. Narcotics addicts in the sense of those devoted to heroin or morphine or some of the more powerful narcotic drugs will take barbiturates occasionally when they are unable to get a supply of morphine or heroin or something of that kind. Barbiturates are to some degree a substitute, and taking them lessens the withdrawal symptoms which a narcotics addict experiences when he cannot obtain his normal dosage of a narcotic, or his next fix, as the expression is. The effect of barbiturates on the individual concerned is somewhat the same as the effect of morphine or heroin as far as withdrawal symptoms are concerned.
Barbiturates have an effect on the personality of the individual who takes them in somewhat the same way as alcohol affects some individuals by changing their personality and attitude from one of mildness and quietude to one of furiousness, filled with a desire to fight or destroy something. The effect of barbiturates is such that one's personality generally is changed. The effect of amphetamine is, I understand, somewhat different in this regard. There, the effect is one of producing hallucinations. I believe a

Food and Drugs Act
number of truck drivers resort to dexedrine or stay awake pills or benzedrine in order to prevent them falling asleep while driving trucks. But, by using these tablets, or whatever they are, they report seeing all kinds of strange objects and items on the road in front of them. According to medical opinion the so-called goof balls are as insidious and dangerous, if not more so, than narcotics themselves, which are dealt with under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act.
There is certainly no regulation or control provided in this bill, as it exists, in respect of the use or distribution of these drugs. I have serious doubt whether it will solve the basic question in respect of the use of barbiturates. While it is true that notice of a motion appeared this morning in routine proceedings and orders of the day regarding the introduction of a bill to provide for the control of narcotic drugs, which will put into effect a policy statement made a few months ago, I expect there will be a system established involving the use of clinics, hospitals or institutions for the segregation and treatment of narcotic drug addicts. This kind of a program has been lacking in this country, as well as in other countries of the world, for many years. If the proposed policy in respect of the trafficking and addiction of individuals to barbiturates is to be similar to the program followed in respect of heroin and opium, which involves only incarceration, then I am afraid we will not solve this problem. The effect may be the emptying of our penitentiaries of narcotic addicts, by placing them in treatment centres, and filling their vacancies in the penitentiaries with addicts and traffickers of barbiturates. If that is the case, the same problem will exist, because there then will not be segregation of addicts to barbiturates and addicts to narcotics. I would hope that under the proposed bill, in respect of the control of narcotic drug trafficking, a policy will be adopted to segregate these addicts from other prisoners, and that a similar course will be followed in respect to the treatment of barbiturate addicts, and those individuals convicted of trafficking in barbiturates.
I must apologize to the minister for not being here for the whole of his opening statement. I had not expected that this bill would be reached as soon as it was. I should like to make another comment in regard to the proposed bill, and perhaps the minister will make some explanation, if he has not already done so.
I understand that when an individual is convicted summarily or on indictment, the penalty will be 18 months and 10 years' imprisonment respectively. After considering

that portion of this proposed bill, I have concluded that is not the case, but that an individual convicted on indictment will be liable to imprisonment up to 10 years. That is, from one year to 10 years, depending upon the discretion of the courts. I understand the individual is also liable to a fine in addition to a term of imprisonment. I should like the minister to explain that portion of the bill, in order to clear up any misunderstanding in this regard.
There is another principle contained in this bill which I feel is rather strange and unique, considering the normal procedures of a court. The bill states that unauthorized trafficking in controlled drugs, as the bill refers to them, is illegal. However, it is my understanding that, under this bill, the possession of these controlled drugs is not illegal. If my understanding of this portion of the bill is accurate, then an individual charged with trafficking, which is the only offence in this respect, who does not plead guilty, will be tried on the same basis as an individual in possession of controlled drugs. That seems very strange to me, in view of the fact that it is not an offence to be in possession of these barbiturates. I presume there is some reason for this principle, and should like the minister to explain it for my benefit.
I understand that if a man is charged with illegal possession of drugs, the onus falls on him to establish one of two things, firstly, that he acquired the drug from a pharmacist or some authorized person; or second, that he was not in possession of the drug for the purpose of trafficking. I suggest it would perhaps be easy to prove the former; that he acquired these drugs from a pharmacist or doctor. However, for what reason could he be in possession of these drugs other than for the purpose of trafficking, unless he was a barbiturate addict? If that were the purpose of his being in possession of them, and in order to prove it, he would then have to establish his source. If he had not obtained the barbiturate from an authorized individual, he must have acquired it in an illegal manner, such as by breaking and entering a drug store, the theft of a doctor's bag, or a theft from some other place. The individual may well have purchased them from an illegal trafficker. By admitting so, he would be admitting another illegal act. I suggest this placing of the burden of proof upon the accused individual is rather an unfair approach to the problem. If the individual charged pleads not guilty to trafficking, then in all likelihood he must admit guilt in respect of another illegal act. I should like to know what benefit he will then derive from this admission?
Will the hon. member permit a question? I was wondering whether the hon. member had thought of the protection of the Canada Evidence Act?

Yes, I had. Since I am not a lawyer I have to take the advice of people who are lawyers. Sometimes this leads one astray, Mr. Speaker; but I have been told that the protection under the Canada Evidence Act-and I was about to come to this-applies only to protection with respect to questions asked. A person is not being asked questions under those circumstances; he is voluntarily taking action to prove his innocence. Thus I say he does not have protection under the Canada Evidence Act in this regard. When we get to this particular point what will be required will be another sort of legal fiction. We have engaged in one example of that already. The minister said that the court will proceed as if the individual had been charged with something else which is not an offence under the act. In committee we should also make an amendment bringing in another sort of legal fiction to the effect that if in the course of establishing that he had those controlled drugs not for the purpose of trafficking his responses would be deemed to be as if he had been asked such questions, and he would be given the same protection under the Canada Evidence Act as if he had been asked those particular questions.
As I say, this was the advice given to me by a member of the legal profession. I know how out of sorts those gentlemen are one with the other at times and how easy it is for them to come to a disagreement over something, particularly law, or what statute law means. I think this would be the effect of one of the principles of this legislation. If an individual were charged with an offence and attempted to prove his innocence he might incriminate himself, or might be in a position possibly to incriminate himself, depending on other circumstances, with respect to his argument of proof. I say that if this is the effect of the part of the bill dealing with the prosecution and the approach in court, then it is unique and strange and a rather dangerous way to proceed. It is something that we might deal with in detail when we get into committee on the bill. I believe it is part of the principle of the bill itself because it deals with the process used to decide whether or not an individual is guilty.
In essence, Mr. Speaker, I think the bill is commendable in the things that it seeks to do. If government policy is merely to stop at this and to take no steps in the field of segregation of those sentenced under the legislation, and no steps in the field of treatment of barbiturate addicts, as is apparently going
Food and Drugs Act
to be done with narcotic addicts, then I think it is a failure. By this I do not mean that the bill itself is a failure, but there is failure on the part of the government to proceed fully in the direction of treatment and segregation, which is the thing that we want to get to.
If we leave the matter here, perhaps the minister will be able to clear up some of the doubts in my mind when he closes the debate, or perhaps we may have to engage in further questioning and discussion about the matter at the committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few brief words on this bill at this time. I am interested in its provisions. I shall have comments to make when we come to the various clauses. I should like to assure the minister that, as the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) has said, we join with him in his efforts to provide a satisfactory form of regulation with regard to the traffic in controlled drugs, which as he said exists in communities where there is an underworld.
First of all, I should like to say-and I had hoped that the minister would say this-we are especially grateful to the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean for being almost single-handedly responsible for the introduction of this measure. It was the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean who three or four years ago first raised this question in the House of Commons. We all recall the derision that greeted his interrogations and his remarks when he referred to this problem of the goof ball.
Oftimes individual members of parliament may feel frustrated in their efforts. They may feel they are not given an opportunity to provide constructive contributions in our deliberations and decisions. However, this is a very good example of how effective an individual member of parliament can be if he puts forward consistently a case which he sincerely believes in. I know of no finer example of achievement in this regard than the results which we see here today in the introduction by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) on behalf of the government of a measure which has been necessitated by circumstances which were first effectively demonstrated in this house by the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean. I am sure I have every justification for extending to him our warmest thanks and our sincerest congratulations.
I have before me:
