The minister has given us a useful outline. With the general statement he has made I think we would be in full agreement. I had at first wondered why the bill was brought forward in this particular form. I had wondered why the subject had not been included in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, but I am satisfied that the explanation which the minister has given is one that meets the situation. He points out that the enforcement measures are the same, generally speaking, but I think there are some differences. If one will compare the enforcement provisions of the Food and Drugs Act one will find that there are some slight differences but basically, as the minister has said, the enforcement measures are the same. While this is so, the minister suggests, and I think rightly so, that since goof balls-and I prefer to use the phrase used in the bill, which is controlled drugs-are not narcotics, on that account they should be treated separately. He points out that the medical use of narcotics is different from that of controlled drugs. He indicates further that the medical profession is against the characterization of barbiturates as narcotics, and I think that the opinion of the medical profession in this regard is one that should be respected because the use of narcotics under legitimate circumstances and under the control of the skilled practitioner is altogether different from the uses which attend the employment of a barbiturate or a controlled drug.
The minister also points out that under the act dealing with narcotics the mere possession of a narcotic is a punishable offence whereas I note that in the bill, and I do not quarrel with this, the mere possession of a controlled drug is not necessarily an offence. The new section 33 (1) on page 2 of the bill deals with this aspect of the problem. That,

I think, is almost in itself a good reason for the particular and special form to which the minister has resorted in this legislation.
He points out that narcotics, unlike controlled drugs or barbiturates, are not normally kept in the home, that they are under the strictest supervision of the doctor and other agencies of the public authority. He indicates as well that barbiturates are transferable from one member of a family to another, from one individual to another, in spite of the fact that the person whom the barbiturate is first given acquires it as the result of a prescription.
I am sure we are satisfied beyond doubt from what the minister has said, and particularly from the facts that have been elicited from time to time in the house by the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean, as to the great abuse that has flowed in recent times from these kind of controlled drugs, especially, in large communities, where the extent of criminality is so often characteristic of the large urban centres on this continent. Undoubtedly the minister and his officers have given this matter very careful attention. I am sure he has acted after the closest examination of the best way to deal with this problem. I can understand very well what some of his difficulties have been because there is a fundamental difference between a narcotic and a controlled drug within the meaning of this legislation and one would not want to do injustices in legitimate situations although one is actuated, as the minister and his officials are, by the need to see to it that the greatest supervision exists not only with regard to the illicit use of narcotic drugs but with regards to the use of barbiturates or controlled drugs.
One could go over a list of many illustrations that have appeared in the press which I have in my possession and which show the extent of the degradation that has taken place recently, particularly in some of our larger centres, as a result of the clandestine use and later the open use of barbiturates by unconscionable individuals exercising influence in particular over some of our young people. This is a necessary measure at this stage and we will examine the bill clause by clause in the hope that we will enact a measure capable of arresting this problem to the extent that it is practicable and possible to do so. Once again I am grateful to the minister and the government for bringing this measure forward. I am sure I also express the gratitude and appreciation of all members of the house for the perception and persistent interest of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the minister for bringing forward this legislation to

cope with this problem and at the same time I should also like to record my appreciation of the untiring efforts of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) to keep this problem before the house and to have some action taken. As I listened to the minister opening the debate two points came to my mind which I should like to put before him for his consideration when he replies.
We have recognized that a problem exists and we are attempting in this legislation to find a solution to the problem by the indirect method, that is, by eliminating the illegal traffic in the drugs involved. The first thought that came to my mind as I considered the matter was that the illicit trade did not begin with the problem. The problem started in some other way and the illicit trade grew out of the problem. As more and more young people became addicted the demand for drugs of this kind grew and the illicit trade grew out of that demand. It is true that we are perhaps going to be very successful in cutting off the illegal sources of supply but that does not automatically cut off the demand. The demand has been created and will be there, so we are now faced with two problems, I believe.
The first problem is, what are we going to do with those people who have become addicted and can no longer get the drugs to meet the demands of their addiction? Obviously they will need some sort of special treatment, and I am wondering whether the minister has given any thought to that part of the problem and whether any research has been carried out as to what kind of treatment is necessary and how it should be provided. The second thought that came to my mind was that this problem started in a very simple way with drugs that could be acquired in a legal manner and although we are attempting, and I think we will perhaps be very successful, to eliminate the illegal sources of supply and to make it more difficult to obtain these drugs from legal sources the problem will not be entirely removed. I think it is reasonable to assume that young people who have become accustomed to this kind of addiction will experiment with other drugs which perhaps can be obtained legally.
It was my impression that this problem started first with simple aspirin and coke. I have been told that, but I do not know how valid the statement is. There are many drugs that are available over the counter without a prescription which possibly could be used as substitutes for the drugs named in this bill.
One other thought which came to my mind was whether any research had been conducted 90205-6-354
Food and Drugs Act
with respect to drugs that might be obtainable without a prescription which could possibly be used as substitutes for the drugs which we are now seeking to control and to eliminate, and which are being supplied from illegal sources.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few brief comments on this bill. First of all, I should like to say that I agree entirely with the principle of this bill. I believe that in a number of centres across this country we have had a goof ball problem among our younger people which, if allowed to go uncontrolled, would not only reach the serious proportions it has reached at this particular time but would become much more serious in areas where the problem exists now and would also spread to a number of other areas.
I suppose that before the minister introduced this bill, most of us thought the use of these barbiturates could be controlled by adding these particular drugs to the narcotics act. The explanation the minister has given is one which I appreciate, and I think we can easily understand that this problem could be better handled and better solved by having a separate bill, as the minister has done. Over the years we have heard the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) complaining about the use of goof balls in the area from which he comes as well as in other areas. It was quite evident he took a much more serious view of the problem at that time than many other people. As a result of his experience with the problem and because of his interest in young people, he persisted and we have before us today a bill which I hope will control the use of these drugs by all people, particularly by the young people.
It is felt that we shall be able to effectively control the use of these drugs by having control of importation, distribution and retail centres. It will be necessary for people in these three different branches of the drug business to keep the necessary records which the bill will demand of them. I hope that this, in some way, will control release of these drugs. I would hope too, Mr. Speaker, that this bill will receive examination in the committee when the different items will be examined, and I would hope that it would be given speedy passage through the house so that its effect will be felt across this country as soon as possible.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-17, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of myself and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) I should like to thank all members of this house for their forbearance and for the privilege of moving the second reading of Bill No. S-17, respecting Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
The purpose of this bill is to authorize Canadian Pacific Railway Company to construct a branch line of railway off its Brocket southerly branch in the province of Alberta to a gas-processing plant being constructed by Shell Oil Company of Canada Limited. Parliamentary authority is necessary because the power of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada to authorize the construction of branch lines under the Railway Act, section 183, is limited to lines not exceeding six miles in length.
The length of this particular branch line is 10.8 miles, and it will start about 1.5 miles north of Drywood which is the present site of the British American Oil Company plant south and east of Pincher Creek, about 17 miles.
To those who are not familiar with the area, let me say that the new Shell plant which is contemplated and on which construction has started is approximately 14 miles south of Pincher Creek and eight to ten miles west of the present British American Oil Company plant. This British American Oil Company plant supplies the methane gas which to a large extent is transported by Trans-Canada Pipe Line to Ontario to warm Ontario homes. In other words, this is the area from which the gas going to Ontario, or a large part of it, originates. This new Shell Oil plant will also be processing various types of hydrocarbons, and for the benefit of those who are not altogether familiar with the petrochemical industry, allow me to

Private Bills
spend a moment or two dealing with the chemical products which are derived from natural gas. Let me say first of all that if you take the total gas produced in the province of Alberta, about 10 per cent is dry natural gas or methane. It comes out of the ground that way. Ninety per cent is wet natural gas and this has to go through a scrubbing plant and be processed. In that processing, methane is taken off, and it is methane which is put through the pipe line to Ontario. This is the gas which goes into our homes as fuel.
Then there is ethane, propane, butane and hydrogen sulphide, just to give hon. members some idea of the end-products which are derived from these gases. Take methane, for example. From methane are produced rubber additives, carbon black, nitrogen fertilizer, antifreeze, plastics, synthetic fibres such as dynel and orlon, explosives, soil conditioners and so on.
Let us look at some of the end-products of ethane. There is first of all, polyethylene plastic, so important to the building trade, synthetic fibres such as dacron, synthetic rubber and detergents, antifreeze and so on.
Now we come to propane. The end-products derived from propane include explosives such as t.n.t., synthetic detergents, films for cameras and for the motion picture industry, lacquers, and so forth. Turning now to butane we have synthetic rubber, nylon, oil additives, synthetic resins and so forth. Lastly, just to touch on some of the products derived from hydrogen sulphide may I say that this new Shell plant which is to be built will produce in the neighbourhood of 1,000 tons per day of sulphur. This is equivalent to about 17 carloads of 60 tons per car, or roughly a small 17-car trainload of sulphur a day. Iri addition, this plant will produce 350 tons of liquid gases which will be transported largely by pipe line. This petrochemical plant and the hydrocarbons which are produced there will provide a raw material source for over 10,000 end-products. I wanted to mention these few things about the petrochemical industry in the west to indicate the necessity for the construction of a railroad line to serve this particular plant. I might add that about 23 per cent of our sulphur requirements are produced in Canada. One petrochemical plant at Medicine Hat uses 135 tons of sulphur a day to make sulphuric acid and, finally, to produce fertilizers with an ammonium base.
This railroad spur line 10.8 miles long is needed to operate the Shell plant economically. Transportation by highway is not practicable because during the winter in that part of the country the snow is deep, and in the

spring when the frost is coming out of the ground there is a tendency for roads to heave. There would be a considerable loss of time in consequence and, in addition, any road which might be expected to stand up to the heavy traffic would be very expensive to construct and maintain. The railroad will help the C.P.R. to produce revenue and it will help the Shell Oil Company of Canada by providing transportation for its products and also in getting building material on to the site to build the plant. The Canadian Pacific Railroad has right of way options already completed. The Shell company has sufficient raw material to last approximately 50 years. Considerable employment will be provided by the building of this line, and it will be available as soon as this house can pass the present measure which is the green light needed for the company to go ahead with construction work.
I want to say one word about the urgency of getting this railroad under construction. There is nothing controversial about the bill, but it has been delayed and delayed by the procedures of this house. What is happening is that these people who have only a short period in the summer in which to construct this railroad are being denied the full opportunity to take advantage of the open season of the year during which construction can go forward. Delays in the house are holding it up.
There were no delays.

I may say it is not the fault of the C.P.R. that this bill is delayed in reaching the floor of this house. Let me clarify that situation. The energy board which was set up by the parliament of Canada and which has done an excellent job in determining the export of gas had to go through all its processes of deciding whether or not the gas could be exported. This had to be done before the Shell oil company could decide to build a plant south of Pincher Creek. The Shell company had to obtain a decision from the energy board before they could set up plans for this $20 million plant south of Pincher Creek. How could the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other group, come before this house making an application for the passage of a bill authorizing the building of a railway line in this respect until the Shell oil company had made its decision? If you follow my line of reasoning, you will see that the C.P.R. was held up by the decision of the Shell oil company and that the Shell oil company was held up by the decision of the national energy board. The national energy board, of course is an agent of the government of Canada and although I do not wish to

attach blame to anyone I certainly feel that neither the C.P.R. nor the Shell oil company is to blame for any delay.
All I am suggesting is that we have here a bill that is urgent, and which should be passed immediately, but which has been held up for three weeks to a month by the procedures of this house. Since this bill is not controversial, I hope that this house will deal with it expeditiously. If the project involved the construction of only six miles of line, construction could have proceeded under the authorization contained in section 183 of the Railway Act. All that is involved here is the construction of a 10.8 mile spur to be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway under the authorization of the board of transport commissioners. The construction of this line cannot begin until this bill receives third reading. I should hope that this house, with its usual sound judgment, will expedite the passage of this bill, which I am sure will be appreciated.

Mr. Speaker, we in this group are very interested in this bill and can assure the member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) that we have no desire whatever to hold it up.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Macleod for the information he gave this afternoon. It has been of particular value to those members who represent ridings in eastern Canada. We are always interested in receiving information in respect of the production of gas in the Alberta region, and the information given in this regard by that hon. member has certainly underlined the sense of urgency which he has indicated.
I was somewhat concerned regarding his meaning when he said that it was delayed by the procedure of this house. I understand the bill was introduced in the other place on April 27, and has progressed at a speed which I imagine is normal. Perhaps the hon. member for Macleod would indicate further what he meant by the delays he suggests have taken place.
The purpose of this bill is quite clear. It is simply to construct an 11 mile spur line from a C.P.R. spur line, which already exists, from a gas well property of the British American Oil Company to the Shell Oil Company. We are very interested in this project because it involves a railway line leading to a field of natural resuorce in this nation. As will be appreciated, we in this group are very interested in natural resources, and are very pleased that this line will run to a gas processing plant, and that this natural resource of Canada is to be processed in Canada by Canadians for Canadians. That is one of the reasons why we greet this particular bill with considerable enthusiasm.

We note that, unless this kind of transportation is provided, it is almost impossible to get these by-products to market. It is quite evident that road conditions in Alberta, during winter months, make highway transport impossible, and air transportation for this purpose is far too expensive. We sincerely hope this railway line will play an important part in the development of the province of Alberta.
We note also, especially after the remarks of the hon. member for Macleod, that there is a tremendous need for the by-products which this company will proceed to process as soon as the plant is built, and the railway spur constructed. It is our understanding that this company will eventually produce many thousands of tons of sulphur. We hope, moreover, that this will be a paying line.
We are about to take a new look at the whole spectrum of Canadian transportation, with special consideration regarding the national problem in respect of railway transportation. The suggestion has been put forward that railway transportation must begin to cut down, and we must concern ourselves only with trunk lines. I am sure all members of this group expect the railway companies in Canada to continue to build lines to the locations of national resources in this country, and that this will be one of the major concerns of the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway, as it is of the directors of the Canadian National Railways. As long as this reaching out for resources continues, we can be assured that employment opportunities will continue to increase.
The fact that this bill has reached the floor of this house indicates the complexity of our economic system, in that even the Canadian Pacific Railway, a so-called private enterprise company, must bring its plans before this house for approval. We realize, however, that the resources of this nation are being marshalled in support of this railway line, and in support of all others.
The hon. member mentioned that employment would be created through the construction of this line. We must question this statement, however, because we noted from both the speech he made this afternoon, and the explanation given previously in respect of the bill, that employment will be provided by the construction of this line for only 25 individuals, which indicates to us the extent to which machinery is replacing manpower in the construction of projects such as railway lines. However, we hope that employment will result in yet another way, as a result of the processing plant being constructed, and through the long term transportation of these materials to areas where they will be of use to the citizens of Alberta and to the nation

as a whole. We hope this will provide employment in some measure, and a boost to the economic growth of our society.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up any extra time in this house, although I should like, by way of emphasis, to reiterate some of the things mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt).
The hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) suggested that the construction of this line would employ only 25 men. In this regard I should like to remind him that the construction of that line represents only one stage of the project. I understand one other stage of construction will employ 100 men, and when the whole project is in operation, many more men than that will be employed. As a matter of fact, the laying of the road is to be done by contract and will provide work for approximately 25 men, but the construction of the road itself will employ 100 men for approximately six months. Of course, an additional number of men will be employed by the Shell oil company.
By way of emphasis, I should also point out the great and immediate need of the nitro-chemical plant at Medicine Hat for sulphur in particular, in the production of a fertilizer with an ammonium base, as well as the immediate need in respect of those other things previously mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod. I suggest that everything that can be done to speed the passage of this bill authorizing the construction of this line should be done, particularly because of the very short season involved.
I do not have much experience in this house and certainly I am not greatly familiar with its proceedings, but I am sure there is a general feeling of co-operation in respect of the passage of this bill, for which I express my appreciation to all hon. members. I should like to join with other members in urging that this bill be dealt with, and put on its way, as quickly as possible, so that the construction of this line may commence at the earliest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a word or two in regard to this bill. I am sure all hon. members appreciate very much the explanations given by the hon. members for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) and for Lethbridge (Mr. Gundlock) in respect of its purpose, and their emphasis regarding the need of speedily dealing with the bill. I hope I am incorrect in thinking that the hon. member for Macleod made reference, on at least one occasion, to delays caused by the proceedings of this house. If that hon.

member actually used those words, I hope he did not do so in a sense of criticism of this house itself.

May I correct the statement which the hon. member has just made. What I had reference to in the matter of delays was the fact that private bills come up only once a week. They are dealt with for one hour once a week. I was not referring to any delays on the part of any group or any individuals in this house. I was referring to the order of business under which such a bill proceeds before it can become law.

That is fine; I was sure that this is what was meant, Mr. Speaker. The bill was introduced in the house on May 5, having come over from the Senate. That was a Friday. On the following Tuesday, May 9, we dealt with a supply motion. There was a supply motion before the house which overrode the private members' hour from five to six, and it was not possible for the bill to come up at that time. This is the third private members' hour on a Tuesday that we have had since the particular bill was introduced, and there were other matters before it. I can appreciate, when only one hour is given to a discussion of those bills, that it is somewhat difficult to proceed with everything that hon. members wish to have proceeded with, and to do it within that one hour.
The request of the hon. member that we waive the rules, following second reading which require that such bills go automatically to a committee and then proceed in committee of the whole and following that give unanimous consent to third reading is a somewhat far reaching request. Perhaps it should not be done at this stage, but I think one should express objection because not much is known about the bill at the present time. I think we should express some concern about following this particular course with respect to a private bill dealing with a private company. We know the reason for the rule, Mr. Speaker. The rule which states that a private bill goes automatically to an appropriate committee is one which recognizes that private citizens who are not members of parliament and are not able to appear before parliament or before the committee of the whole, can go to one of the standing committees of the house and present their ideas to hon. members in a formal way. It would seem to me that to give consent out of hand, as it were, to waive the rules is something that would not be correct. I think it requires very careful examination. There is one way in which we might even help in that regard in getting the opinions of the railway officials themselves

and perhaps of the Shell oil company. At this time I am not saying that the hon. member for Macleod did not adequately perform his function as sponsor of the bill. I think he did a commendable job and gave a thorough explanation of what would occur once this bill was passed.
The bill was referred to the Senate standing committee on transport and communications. I assume that the railway officials appeared before that committee and answered questions, as is done on other occasions with respect to other bills. They perhaps answered questions which were in the minds of the members of the Senate when the bill was given second reading. Sometimes we in this house, Mr. Speaker, look to the proceedings of the other place and of the committees of the other place for explanations and information. In this instance we are prevented from doing that because no evidence was taken down and transcribed and printed by the standing committee of the other place on transport and communications which dealt with this particular bill. I am not saying this by way of criticism of the other place or of the committees of the other place; I am merely saying that normally we might look to the proceedings there and get some explanation and some answers to some of the questions that might be in our minds. But we are not able to do this because evidence was not taken down and transcribed in the committee of the other place.
There are one or two questions in my mind which the hon. member for Macleod may be able to clear up when he closes the debate. I believe I am correct in saying that he said that about 10 per cent of the gas was dry, and I gather from this that 90 per cent of the gas in that part of the province is considered to be wet gas. I do not know whether he was talking about the whole province. I understand that by this particular legislation the Shell company will be serviced by this proposed railway spur, and the company will be processing wet gas from that general area. In this wet gas there are large quantities of sulphur, propane, butane and the like. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that when we get into the field of propane and butane we have in mind another private bill dealing with a pipe line company which is before the committee at the present time. I do not want to enter into a discussion of it because it is another subject of debate. I merely say there is a similarity between the two in that one has to do with exporting certain products and this one, as I understand it, has to do with a rail line to a plant which will be processing these wet gases and producing some useable commodities in Canada rather than exporting raw material.
Private Bills
I understand that the plant mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod which is to be built will have a production capacity of 1,000 tons of sulphur a day. In 1956, when we did not have sufficient production facilities, apparently, we imported some 270,000 tons of sulphur. If this Shell plant, which is to be serviced by the proposed rail spur, should produce 1,000 tons a day and operate on a seven day week basis the full 12 months of the year its total annual production would be 365,000 tons, which is a bit more than the amount we imported into Canada in 1956, and a bit more than our present consumption, judging by what we imported in 1956. At that time we had an annual consumption of about 350,000 tons of sulphur. This plant which is apparently going to produce 1,000 tons a day, will be, I gather, the largest sulphur production plant in Canada. Apparently our past production in Canada was 23 per cent of our consumption but there is nothing with which to equate 1956.
I would hope that the Shell Oil company has some contracts or other companies have options for the purchase of sulphur. If we are going to process this wet gas and produce sulphur from it in the amount of 1,000 tons per day, which on a yearly basis is more than our annual consumption and far more than our current annual production, I would hope that the sulphur will be sold and used in Canada by other manufacturers rather than being exported in its raw state, as it were, from our country to other places for other purposes as happens with other commodities we produce.
When the hon. member for Macleod closes the debate on second reading I would appreciate it very much if he would clear up the point as to just what markets Shell Oil has. I realize that this matter is something apart from the bill before us in which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company seeks permission to build 10.8 miles of rail line, but the hon. member for Macleod mentioned the Shell Oil company, its prospective production and so on and if he has that information I think it would certainly be helpful to the house.
Along the same lines, I think it would be helpful if the hon. member could indicate what existing markets Shell Oil has for the other by-products, I believe they might be called, developed in the processing of the wet gas. He mentioned the propanes and butanes that could be developed. If he has the information, I should also like the hon. member to indicate where the market is that Shell Oil has for the gas that will be produced if in fact Shell Oil is going to be the distributing firm.

Private Bills
I think these are all important matters in the light of our ideas and concepts with regard to the development of industry in Canada and the using of our raw materials in Canada for Canadian production and consumption. Because I think everyone in the house feels the same way, I think it is important that we understand just what Shell Oil intends to do with these products once the C.P.R. has constructed the rail line to the plant and Shell Oil is able to ship out the products. What markets will Shell Oil have? I think this is a very important question and I should like to see it cleared up in as much detail as possible before we consider whether or not we should waive the rules and proceed with the other stages of the bill in the house without referring it to a standing committee.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the committee is by itself a very simple one in that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is merely asking for authority to build a railway line approximately 11 miles in length. A bill is necessary because of the provision in the Railway Act that the authority of parliament is required for the construction of any branch railway line more than six miles in length.
But the bill is an interesting one in that it appears to be an integral part of a development in the west, one that I think should commend itself to all hon. members. I was quite sympathetic to the hon. member in his request, as I understood him, that the house concur in moving the bill forward through all stages today and if he wishes to put that proposition to the house in a formal way at a later stage I for my part am quite agreeable to such a suggestion.
I took the trouble to try to inform myself as best I could with respect to the development that will be consequential upon the C.P.R. being granted authority to build this branch line and upon the completion of the line, and while this matter may not be strictly relevant to the discussion of whether or not the bill should be approved it certainly is interesting. We have here a recently discovered natural resource in this country where the proven reserves of gas are estimated to be sufficient to supply the needs of the company proposing to develop them for 50 years at the contemplated rate of development. We have the assurance that the company proposes to commence development immediately the railway line is built.
It seems to me that all in all this is exactly what is needed at this time when all hon. members are concerned about the necessity of developing our country, providing employment for our manpower and using our resources in such a way that we will terminate

the existing unemployment. Therefore this development is wholly desirable. I content myself simply by indicating concurrence in the bill on my own behalf and on behalf of those immediately around me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must inform the house that if the hon. member for Macleod speaks now he will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. members who have spoken to the bill for their sympathetic understanding of the situation in which we find ourselves. I was particularly interested in the questions asked by the hon. member for Skeena concerning wet gas and dry gas. I mentioned that 10 per cent of the gas in the province of Alberta generally was dry gas, but in the field south of Pincher Creek where the Shell plant is located, it is 100 per cent wet gas and the gas processed there will be wet gas.
As to the markets for sulphur, let me say that sulphur is exported to world markets through the bulk loading facilities at Vancouver to some extent. It is shipped to Italy and other countries of the world where it is one of the principal ingredients in the production of synthetic fibres. In other words, it is impossible to produce synthetic fibres without the use of sulphuric acid. A great deal of sulphur is shipped into the Canadian shield region of our north country where sulphuric acid is needed to separate certain minerals from the rock formation. It is also used, as I have mentioned, in the production of ammonium-base fertilizer at the plant at Medicine Hat. It is also shipped to other parts of the world where there are other fertilizer plants. It is used in the production of storage batteries.
We are dealing with an extremely complicated situation in that most of the various products to be shipped such as ethane, propane, butane and hydrogen sulphide, when in the form of liquid gases, are shipped by pipe line.
Now, these gases are a drug on the market. It is difficult to get rid of them. It is felt that there is a market in the United States for some. We have an abundant supply. In fact, we have such a supply of these particular by-products that it is impossible to utilize them in Canada for petrochemical purposes. In other words, if we were to set up petrochemical plants we would have an untold number of years ahead of us of utilization of these by-products. In addition, these by-products which 1 have mentioned, ethane, propane and butane as well as certain other hydrocarbons, can be obtained from the

petroleum industry. They can also be obtained from coal, and we have over seven per cent of the coal supply of the world in southwestern Alberta.
What I wish to emphasize is that these particular hydrocarbons are in surplus supply. They are usually conveyed to market by pipe line, and the Aurora pipe line was one of the means by which it was hoped a certain amount of them would be transported across the line. I am not going to get into a discussion of Aurora pipe line. I want to avoid that. But I do want to say, in so far as the market situation is concerned, that where there is such an abundant supply, the practice in the industry is to apply to the conservation board of the province of Alberta to have certain of the gases flared. We do not want that if we can possibly find markets. Let us therefore find markets and utilize these products.
In closing the debate, I should like to urge upon you the thought that there is a precedent for this particular bill. I should like to see it given passage here today. I have already impressed upon hon. members the urgency of moving the bill through the house as quickly as possible. The bill has been cleared by the Senate and we have a record of the evidence given there. I have tried to give hon. members every bit of detail. There is nothing to cover up, there is nothing to hide. The bill relates simply to the construction of 10.8 miles of a branch line off another branch line to allow this company to go ahead with its plans. There is no great, deep principle involved, simply common, ordinary horse sense in order to get this project under way and to get things moving in that part of the country.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

Mr. Speaker, I understand that a few years ago the British-American Oil Company received consideration similar to that which I am going to request. I should like to move that, notwithstanding standing order 105, unanimous consent be given to referring this Bill No. S-17, to the committee of the whole.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member will require unanimous consent before such a motion can be entertained. Standing order 105 requires that every private bill, when read a second time, be referred to one of the standing committees. This particular bill would be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Standing order 102 reads:
No motion for the suspension or modification of any provision of part II of the standing orders applying to private bills or to petitions for private
Private Bills
bills shall be entertained by the house until after reference is made to the committee on standing orders, or to one of the committees charged with the consideration of private bills,-
There are, therefore, two standing orders standing in the way of the motion. However, as everyone knows, the house is master of its own procedure. If unanimous consent were given to the hon. member to move the appropriate motion, then the bill could be advanced.
The question is whether the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Kindt) has unanimous consent of the house to move the suspension of the two standing orders in question in order to advance this bill to committee of the whole house.
Before it is agreed, I think it should be clearly understood this is in no way to be considered as any sort of precedent of which advantage can be taken in future proceedings.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I take it the hon. member is. consenting, subject to this caveat.
Is it agreed that the hon. member has. unanimous consent to move this motion?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Perhaps an appropriate motion would be as follows:
Mr. Kindt, seconded by Mr. Gundlock, moves that the said bill be considered forthwith in committee of the whole house.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Motion agreed to and the house went into, committee thereon, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Line of railway authorized.

I do not wish to delay the passage of the bill. I listened with great interest to the eloquent appeal for the building of 11 miles of steel. I want to come back to the railroad now. Will this 11 miles of siding, as it is called, serve other shippers if it should happen that other natural resources are discovered or agricultural products are available for shipment? Will this railroad be a public utility, in other words? Or will it only be a siding? There is a difference between the two in so far as restrictions are concerned. Will there be any passenger service on this approximately 11 miles of railroad? Have easements been obtained and settled with all those persons whose land this railway crosses and have the crossings of rights of way been sanctioned by the board of transport commissioners?

With regard to the last question, I understand that the crossings have been cleared with the municipalities and with the board of transport commissioners as well

Private Bills
as with the provincial highways department. In so far as the highway south of Pincher Creek is concerned, there is to be an overhead bridge and not a level crossing.
With reference to passenger service on the line, I may say it is only a spur line. I understand that there was a passenger train run down there on an excursion trip carrying a number of the officials of the B-A plant. Perhaps a similar use will be made of the railroad from time to time. I do not believe that passenger service up to Brocket would be a matter for consideration.
In so far as the public utility aspect is concerned, I can assure the hon. member after discussion with the Canadian Pacific Railway officials that if they can make a dollar out of transporting any products over that line they are going to do so.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.
On clause 2-Time for completion.

Can the hon. member explain the reason for this clause? It says:
If the construction of the said line of railway is not commenced within a period of two years or is not completed and put in operation within a period of five years after the passing of this act, the powers of construction hereby conferred upon the company shall cease and be null and void as regards so much of the said line of railway as shall then remain uncompleted.
Why is that clause included? It seems rather unusual.

That is the standard clause that is put in all bills of this type coming before parliament. While that clause is put in there, the only thing it amounts to is this. The C.P.R. has the intention of getting this railroad built this summer or before the snow flies this fall. But this is one of the clauses that are put in bills of this type, as will be seen by the hon. member if he looks at other bills. That is standard procedure.

I understood the hon. member to say that this is the standard clause that goes into any bill of this nature for the building of a railway line. But is this so with regard to all lengths of line? Suppose the proposed railway line were intended to take 10 years to construct. Are the times different?

It is possible that those drafting the bill might vary the time mentioned in this clause to fit the circumstances. But as I have said this is a 10.8 mile railroad spur line and it is to be built very soon. I checked with the board of transport commissioners on the point raised by the hon. member and the answer they gave me is what I have transmitted to the hon. member for Kootenay West.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Clause agreed to.

Preamble agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

speechtext: When shall the bill be read a third time?
Now.

the third reading of the bill.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Tuesday, May 16, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-2, to incorporate Aurora Pipe Line Company- Mr. Woolliams-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
On clause 1-Incorporation.

This is one of those bills that you lose track of once in a while because other proceedings intervene. Questions are raised and some two or three weeks later you get an opportunity to see whether or not the particular questions have been answered. At an earlier stage in the discussion of this particular bill I raised a number of points which have not yet been clarified, to my mind. I think they should be clarified and explained and that adequate information should be given before we proceed further with this bill.
There has been a great deal of discussion about the ownership of this company and letters have been written by Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited officials about the ownership of this company and the distribution of the shares as between Canadian citizens and non-Canadian citizens. The question is what is Continental Oil's position with

respect to its ownership of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas. It will be recalled that Continental Oil is a United States company and that it holds, or at least did so at the time this matter was discussed earlier-there may have been some slight change since that time-67.77 per cent of Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas submitted some information with respect to Canadian ownership which, if I recall it correctly, amounted to some 2.96 per cent; I refer to individual Canadian ownership in Hudson's Bay. What I should very much like to know is this. I should like to have some confirmation of it from Continental Oil or from someone who can obtain the information from them or from Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company. Has any information been given to that company by its parent owner? As to Continental Oil which now owns 67.77 per cent of Hudson's Bay which owns Aurora Pipe Line Company which is seeking permission to build this pipe line under the bill, is it the intention of Continental Oil to dispose of its ownership of these shares or its percentage of shares in Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company? If we can get some information with regard to that matter, I think it may help a great deal in resolving this question of foreign ownership of a company which will own Aurora or Canadian ownership.

So soon?

speakerposition: topic
subtopic
