speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-99, to amend the Food and Drugs Act-Mr. Monteith (Perth)-Mr. Flynn in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 7.30 p.m.
On clause 1-Exports.

May I ask the
minister what his reaction is to the suggestion that in section 31(c) after the word "import" should be added-I am suggesting for the purpose of argument-the word "export".

While the minister is considering that point I thought he might wish
Food and Drugs Act
to examine at the same time the relevant position of the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act which deals in great detail with the definition of traffic and trafficking. I was wondering why that definition was not incorporated into the Food and Drugs Act because as the hon. member for Essex East has pointed out, the word "export" has been omitted from this clause. I presume that is because these barbiturates are not manufactured in Canada at the present time. However, I think we might reach the stage where they could be manufactured here. I also was wondering why the word "distribution" which is also contained in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act was not included. I thought the very wide definition of traffic and trafficking would be invaluable, besides presenting a degree of legislative uniformity.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I do not think I would have any objection to the word "export" being added there, but I do not believe we need go beyond that at this stage, because this is a new clause dealing with a product which is not a narcotic. A narcotic is a different substance. Under the narcotics act possession is, of course, an offence, whereas it is not an offence under section 3 of the Food and Drugs Act covering so-called goof balls or controlled drugs. The present definition would seem to me to meet the situation and I do not think we need go beyond it. I have not got the definition provided in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act before me with respect to trafficking, but I feel that this one will suffice.

The definition in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act reads:
Traffic or trafficking means the importation, exportation, manufacture, sale, giving, administering, transportation, delivery or distribution by any person of a drug or any substance represented or held out by such person to be a drug, or the making of any offer in respect thereof, but does not include
(i)	the importation or exportation of any drug by or on behalf of any person who has a licence therefor under section 3, or
(ii)	the manufacture, sale, giving, administering, transportation, delivery or distribution of a drug, or the making of any offer in respect thereof, by or on behalf of any person who has a licence therefor under section 3, or by or on behalf of a physician, dentist, veterinary surgeon or retail druggist for a medicinal purpose.
I should think the delivery aspect is one of great importance and I agree with the hon. member for Essex East that the word "export" should be included in the section.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think the hon. member has been looking at the old act. There was a new bill introduced today entitled "an act to provide for the control of narcotic drugs". I think if the hon. member examines that he will find that the definition

Food and Drugs Act
is more or less that which is used in the proposed new act. As far as the inclusion of the word "export" is concerned, there is no reason why this should not be done. The reason it is included in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act is because of the international consequences which might arise. At the moment this international situation has not arisen as far as controlled drugs are concerned.
Would the minister move accordingly?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I will ask my colleague the Solicitor General to move that the word "export" be added after the word "sell" ini line 21.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I so move.

I now have Bill No. C-100 before me. I did not have it when I made my earlier remarks. There, the definition of "traffic" reads:
To manufacture, sell, give, administer, transport, deliver or distribute.
I do not believe the word "distribute" is included in the definition we are at present considering. My only desire, Mr. Chairman, is to reflect the concern we feel in British Columbia where the narcotics problem is an extremely serious one. I wish to make sure that all the loopholes in the act are blocked.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I certainly appreciate the hon. member's concern in this respect, and know he is fully aware of the situation in British Columbia. Perhaps I should give him the definition of the word "sell", as it appears in the Food and Drugs Act, of which this is a part. The word "sell" is described there as including "sell, offer for sale, expose for sale, be in possession for sale, and distribute."
That covers it.

Is it
the committee's wish that I now put the proposed amendment to the committee?
Agreed.

The
hon. member for St. John's West moves:
That section 31 (c) of clause 1 of Bill No. C-99 be amended by inserting after the word "sell'' in line 21, the word "export".
Shall the amendment carry?
Agreed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
Is section 32 of clause 1 agreed to?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise two points in respect of this section,

one in the form of a question, and the other as an expression of opinion. I understand that the ten years' sentence provided upon conviction on indictment is not an automatic sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Oh, no, that is the maximum sentence.
I understand in addition to a jail sentence there can be a fine?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The Criminal Code provides that it is within the court's discretion to provide both a term of imprisonment and a fine.

The other point I wish to raise has to do with a program to be carried out in respect of Bill No. C-100, a copy of which I have not as yet been able to obtain. I understand that the program, as provided by that bill, has regard to the treatment and segregation of addicts and traffickers in narcotic drugs. I should like to suggest at this time, while we are dealing with this bill in respect of the addiction and trafficking in barbiturates, that a similar approach be taken to individuals convicted under the law, as it will be when this bill becomes legislation. It is my understanding that an individual can become addicted to barbiturates and suffer the same withdrawal symptoms, with the same physical and mental state, as individuals who are addicted to opium and heroin. If that is the case, it seems to me that similar steps should be taken to ensure that individuals who are addicted to this controlled class of drugs are also subjected to the same treatment and segregation program that is proposed to be provided in respect of those individuals addicted to opium and heroin, and their derivatives. I wonder whether the minister could indicate to this committee whether a similar program is anticipated under the provisions of this bill?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
There is no provision for specific treatment provided under this bill. The hon. member is entirely right in that respect. This is a new venture and we do not feel there is the need for specific separated treatment in this regard. It is my understanding that the addiction involved in respect of these controlled drugs is not of the same type or degree as in the case of opium or heroin. It has not been felt at this stage that we should provide such specific treatment.
As the hon. member is no doubt aware, there is a new bill-I refer to Bill No. C-100 -in respect of narcotic control, and I think we are heartily in accord with the treatment steps in it. However, in regard to the bill presently before the committee, I feel we

should acquire some experience in this regard, so that we will then have a better appreciation of what is required before taking that step.

Mr. Chairman, this aspect of the problem is of great interest. I had a thought similar to that of the hon. member for Skeena, but suspected the situation might be as the minister has indicated. The minister should not misunderstand me. This is a highly technical aspect of the problem. The minister has at his disposal very well informed professional individuals. I would be very interested in knowing if it is their judgment that the degree of addiction is, as he said, not the same, and that there is no experience which suggests that victims of controlled drugs can be treated in the way in which it is proposed to treat drug addicts, in institutions like the one at Lexington, Kentucky. Is the minister in a position to say whether in Lexington they do or do not treat victims of addiction to controlled drugs, or are only narcotic addicts being treated there? I have the impression there has been a change in that regard, and that the officials of that institution are now attempting to treat, in an experimental way, individuals who are addicted to these so-called controlled drugs. If that is the situation, and as we are about to embark upon a different experimental measure, seeking to provide rehabilitation through detention and hospitalization, it seems to me that, if what is being attempted in Lexington is of any value, we ought to do the same.
Am I right in saying that in California, in the last year or so, there has been created a new institution in an attempt to deal with addicts to controlled drugs, or barbiturates? I am not sure about that suggestion, but it seems that I have read something quite recently in that regard. However, I shall be guided by the minister's final statement on this matter, and I do think the point raised by the hon. member for Skeena is one that we should explore.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two comments in regard to this particular section, dealing with the trafficking of barbiturates, which I consider is perhaps the most nefarious aspect of the whole problem of the illegal use of narcotics. It is my understanding that the trafficker is invariably an individual who does not use the drug himself, but passes it on to other people. It is also my understanding that there is a tendency for younger people to experiment with the use of these barbiturates and narcotic drugs.
The thing that concerns me about this particular clause is the punishment. On summary conviction the term of imprisonment
Food and Drugs Act
is 18 months. Under indictment the term of imprisonment may be 10 years. Under the present Opium and Narcotic Drug Act imprisonment is for a term not exceeding 14 years for trafficking, and there is also a provision for whipping. Under the new Bill No. C-100 a person who is guilty of trafficking is liable to be imprisoned for life. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that we should give very serious consideration to incorporating this more extensive term in this particular clause because I think the experience of the law enforcing agencies has been that the stiffer the term the more likelihood there is that the people who are in this particular business will get out of it.
I think this has been the experience in the United States, particularly with Mafia, which was extremely well organized in the narcotic aspect of the business. As the sentences toughened up this very well organized group tended to get out of the business. With these goof balls which can be added to soft drinks as well as alcohol to produce the effect desired I think there is perhaps even a more serious situation than we have in narcotics. Could the minister indicate the reasoning behind the length of the sentence indicated in this legislation and would he consider making it uniform with the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and provide imprisonment for life?

Before the minister replies I wonder whether the committee would give unanimous consent to improving a slight discrepancy or possibly making an improvement in the wording of the amendment to section 31, which was carried a short time ago? The effect of the amendment was to add to paragraph (c) the word "export" following the word "sell". This would mean that the paragraph would then read:
(c) "traffic" means to manufacture, sell, export, import into Canada-
And so on. The suggestion that I am offering to the committee is that we might add the words "from, or" after the word "export". The paragraph would then read:
(c) "traffic" means to manufacture, sell, export from, or import into Canada, transport or deliver, otherwise-
And so on.
Agreed.

May
I have the permission of the hon. member for St. John's West to add these words to the amendment?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. Thank you very much for pointing it out.

Food and Drugs Act

Is it
unanimously agreed that the amendment which has been carried to section 31 shall have the words "from, or" added to it?
Agreed.

The
paragraph will now read:
(c) "traffic" means to manufacture, sell, export from, or import into Canada, transport or deliver, otherwise than under the authority of this part or the regulations.
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East mentioned possible experiments conducted at Lexington. This is so, so far as barbiturates are concerned. They are individual experiments.
While we are not actually discussing Bill No. C-100, it is realized that in that bill there is provision for special treatment. We feel that this is a new venture, a new step, and that in the case of barbiturates or controlled drugs the situation is not as serious at the moment. We certainly will continue to study it, and if there is a need in the future to provide specific treatment, a specialized sort of treatment, we shall certainly be very pleased to act.
I should like to point out that actually we are dealing with and making punishable only trafficking and possession for the purposes of trafficking. It is not actually possession that we are dealing with; it is just those two things, trafficking or possession for trafficking purposes. This is to quite a degree at the moment being done on the advice of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and their advice, of course, is given after having had considerable experience and making quite a study of the matter over the last several months.
The hon. member for Essex East also mentioned something that was going on in California. I am afraid that at the moment I am unaware of what this might be, but I would mention that in California they have had an experiment concerning free drugs to addicts.
With respect to the comments of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, here again I would point out that we are acting on the advice of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. We do not feel that those penalties should be as severe as they are under the new suggested narcotic control act. First of all, we do not believe for a moment that the courts would impose the type of sentence included in Bill No. C-100 in cases under this particular bill. We realize that it is a serious problem. We are taking a new step to try to deal with it and we hope we can

deal with it. If further steps have to be taken then, of course, we shall take them.
Before I proceed with my main remarks, may I ask the minister whether the drug known as marijuana is included in the schedule to the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes, it is.

I think it will be discovered, or it is probably well known in medical circles anyway, that marijuana is not an addictive drug. It certainly produces a euphoric effect similar to other narcotic drugs. It is an addictive one as we think of the other narcotic drugs as being addictive, and yet a person convicted under the other act for possession, for argument's sake, of marijuana would be liable to be sentenced to a term and the like as would a person convicted for possession of morphine. I just merely say this in opposition, as it were, to the reasoning of the minister with respect to barbiturate addicts when he said that this is not as serious as a person being addicted to other narcotic drugs. As far as marijuana is concerned, it could be far more serious and far more damaging to the individual, according to medical opinion.
Another point which must be considered is that one of the ways in which younger people come in contact with narcotic drugs- and a similar situation will develop with respect to barbiturates or controlled drugs- is that a younger person who has no previous association with narcotics or narcotic addiction may be sentenced for some other offence to a penitentiary or a provincial jail. While there, because of the lack of segregation, he comes into contact with narcotic addicts. The general day to day discussion among narcotic addicts in penitentiary is pointed toward that day when they can get out and get down town and get their first fix, as they call it, or a shot of morphine, or whatever they can get. With many narcotic addicts their sole thought is to get out of prison in order to make use of narcotics again. The process of day-to-day talk and discussion does raise the idea in the minds of younger people that there must be something delightful about the use of narcotics to make these addicts so enamoured of them that this is the first thing they are going to do when they get out. From association in prison with addicts or people who know about narcotics younger people do have a tendency to some extent to try narcotics themselves when they get out of prison if they circulate in the same walk of life.
The same thing will be true with respect to association with barbituric addicts by younger people who are not addicts. Even

though this is initial legislation in this field, unless the minister is willing at this time to place barbituric addicts or traffickers in the same class as narcotic addicts so far as treatment and segregation are concerned, I am very much afraid that we will have a growing problem and a few years from now the minister or another minister will come back again and say that something has got to be done with regard to the treatment of persons using barbiturates. I am quite sure that is what is going to occur.
To my mind it would be much better to have some foresight in regard to the treatment of barbituric addicts and to establish facilities so that individuals can be segregated and treated. The type of treatment may vary. Quite frankly, I think all the psychiatrists in the world will not be of much help to a narcotic addict if the addict desires to use narcotics unless he may be unhappy with his present situation and realizes it is resulting in more difficulty for him than happiness. While we are at the job of establishing machinery for the treatment of narcotic addiction I think we should also establish facilities at the same time for the treatment of barbituric addicts. It may be that the type of treatment will be different and that medical treatment of some kind will be of advantage. It may be some other form of treatment, but at least we should establish facilities for the treatment of barbituric addicts in such a way that they will be segregated from prison inmates convicted of other crimes.
The minister says that he wants to try out this legislation to see how it works but with all due respect I think he will agree without hesitation that it is far better to have some machinery in existence that can be used to overcome a problem which may arise with regard to barbituric addicts than it is to wait until the problem does arise and then say that something must be done after the problem has become greater than it is now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I might say a few words in reply to the statements by the hon. member for Skeena. First of all, while marijuana is in the schedule of the new narcotic control legislation it is regarded internationally as a narcotic and the controlled drugs with which we are dealing in this bill are not. I think it might be pointed out that in our humble opinion this is the most forward step we know of that has been taken in this respect in any country.
In this bill we are not dealing with addicts who use barbiturates or amphetamines or other controlled drugs. We are dealing primarily with the trafficker and those found in possession for trafficking purposes. On the basis of the best advice we have been able
Food and Drugs Act
to obtain it is our feeling that we should develop the control of these drugs and licence all those who handle them with a view to stopping the illicit trade in them. We are also certainly far from convinced that this problem is as serious as narcotic addiction. We are convinced it is not as serious. I am afraid I cannot go along with the hon. member at this stage. After all, narcotic addiction and its serious consequences have been well known for many, many years and the amendment being brought forward in Bill No. C-100 represents actually the first time that this type of approach has been taken toward treatment. In our humble estimation barbiturates do not represent as serious a problem and consequently I am afraid we will have to leave what the hon. member has suggested for another time.

Mr. Chairman, if I understand correctly, the new section 32 covers two types of infractions. The first is trafficking and the second is possession for the purpose of trafficking. If that is so, it means that if a man is caught by the police in possession of a controlled drug such a case is not covered under the new section 32. Am I right in my assumption?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: If a man is in possession-
I mean sole possession without any idea of trafficking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Oh, no, it is not covered. We are not after the users of barbiturates or amphetamines at the moment. These are household drugs in every sense of the word and in most houses practically every medicine cabinet contains some drug of this type. We are not dealing with these people. What we are after is the trafficker in controlled drugs or those found guilty of possession for purposes of trafficking.

If that is so, would the minister not agree that in the enforcement of the narcotics act with regard to the use of heroin, for example, we are in the main controlling the users because it is not very often we are able to catch the trafficker. If the question of controlled drugs is serious enough to warrant an amendment to the Food and Drugs Act, I think there should be a clause in the bill to cover the person who is in possession even if such possession were only punished by a nominal fine. I think that enforcement would be much easier if that were done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot agree with the hon. member. As I mentioned earlier, these drugs are in common everyday

Food and Drugs Act
use on doctor's prescriptions in practically every household. For argument's sake, let us say that an epileptic is out on the street and has a drug of this type in his pocket which he finds it necessary to use upon certain occasions. We do not feel that at this stage we can possibly include straight possession as an offence under the bill. If we can charge a man with possession for trafficking that, of course, is a very different matter. It is the trafficker we are after.

Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to look at subsection 1 of the new section 32. Surely that is a rather anomalous situation. The section provides that no person shall traffic in a controlled drug and "controlled drug" is defined in section 31. Then subsection 1 of section 32 goes on to say, so far as trafficking is concerned:
-or any substance represented or held out by him to be a controlled drug.
It, in fact, might not be a controlled drug. Let us assume a person is selling aspirin. He says, this is a controlled drug. If he were brought to trial his only offence would have been the statement he made that this was a controlled drug. In fact, it is not a controlled drug. How then could he be found guilty of trafficking in something which is not a controlled drug, such as aspirin or a bottle of Coca-Cola? By themselves, they are not controlled drugs.
This section of the bill certainly contains a provision that would not stand up before any court. If the person were trafficking in a controlled drug he could be found guilty. If the evidence shows it is not a controlled drug, you cannot ask for a conviction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this phrase, "any substance represented or held out by him to be a controlled drug", may require a word of explanation. In view of the fact that this offence involves a criminal underworld transaction, it is necessary that undercover activities be employed to reveal the source of the trafficking. This provision is also contained in the narcotics legislation. It is not to be expected that honesty and fair dealing will prevail in illicit underworld trafficking. Someone may be selling sugar, but if he represents it to be a controlled drug, we feel he is part of the underworld and should be charged as such.

I may say that we are dealing now with a well organized group of traffickers. I point out to the minister, for instance, that the head traffickers will call up a drug store, or perhaps even 12 drug stores, and order 100 aspirin tablets from each drug store, while ordering 100 tranquilizers from 12 other stores. He says, in the first place,

deliver these to me at 45 Monterey street, apartment 25. He goes to the doorway of apartment 25 and waits in the entrance hall. When the boy brings the tablets, this man meets him at the door. He does not live there. He takes the 100 aspirin tablets and pays the 98 cents or $1 to the messenger. He then gets in his car and delivers the tablets to another pusher. You cannot catch him because he moves on to another place and does the same thing. He may do this 12 or 15 times in one evening. You can never catch him with the goods because he has only 100 aspirin tablets or 100 tranquilizers, and he passes them on to another fellow. This fellow goes on and distributes these pills. How are you ever going to catch the trafficker who handles goods in that way? He never has 200 pills of any kind at one time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I do not quite understand, Mr. Chairman, what the hon. member is getting at. We are not dealing with aspirin tablets, we are dealing with the drugs outlined in the schedule which are dangerous drugs and which sometimes lead to tragic results. I do not know to what he is referring when he says that one man goes here or there with 100 aspirin tablets.
We do intend now to have all those who handle these three controlled drugs keep records and have them available for inspection. Then we may, upon inspection, determine whether or not there has been any illicit trafficking.

I take it the minister's studies have not gone far enough because I am telling him now what occurs. Anyone knows that you do not need to make these drugs into capsules. All you need to do is mix the two together and you have a goof ball. A goof ball may lead to murder or any other offence if it contaminates any young person. These goof balls enable people to lose all sense of responsibility. If the procedure I have outlined is repeated 12 times, you could never convict a person who dealt with these drugs because he never buys all the products at the same time. If you arrest him you will find him with 100 aspirin tablets. You cannot charge a man for having 100 aspirin tablets. However, if he repeats the transaction 12 or 15 times in one day, he has accumulated enough ingredients to make 1,000 goof balls. You cannot convict him because you never find him with the goods, but only with ordinary drugs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
First of all, may I say I am sure the hon. member realizes that tranquilizers are obtained by prescription. You cannot go into a drug store today and buy tranquilizers without a prescription. I do not

want to belittle the problem. The R.C.M.P. certainly are worried about catching traffickers, and they are thinking of this problem of the addict.
I should like to reiterate what I said earlier, that tranquilizers are not the easiest thing to obtain because they are obtained on prescription.

When I drew the minister's attention to subsection 1, I did so in an effort to close an escape hatch. If the section were to provide that anyone found in possession of a controlled drug or ingredients which could be converted into a controlled drug, it would be much more effective than saying "any substance represented or held out to be a controlled drug". What trafficker is going to say, I am selling you aspirin or tranquilizers which, in themselves, are not controlled drugs but which I tell you are controlled drugs. You cannot convict him unless you have evidence that he represented or held them out to be controlled drugs. No trafficker is going to be so stupid as to admit that what he is selling is not a controlled drug but that he represents it to be a controlled drug.
I therefore, draw the minister's attention to the fact that this clause provides an excellent avenue of escape for anyone who is trafficking in ingredients which could be part of a goof ball, and that such language would be much more effective if it were to say a man could be found guilty if he were in possession of ingredients which could be converted into a controlled drug. I would put it this way. If I were defence counsel I would have a much more difficult time having a man acquitted if he were charged with being in possession of ingredients which could be part of a. controlled drug than attempting to prove that what he was selling was not a controlled drug but that he held it out to be a controlled drug. This would be a fairly easy avenue of escape for defence counsel.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think I understand what the hon. member is trying to get at. He said that any substance could be represented or held out by him to be a controlled drug. As we see this situation, the action will involve underworld characters or they would not be representing themselves to be a pusher or a trafficker, whatever they are called. As a consequence, if he sells something, completes a transaction with a buyer and is found to do this and is charged, he can be charged and found guilty even though the article he has sold is not an actual controlled drug but only was represented by him to be so. In other words, no buyer would buy a capsule, or however these things come, from
Food and Drugs Act
a trafficker unless it had been represented by the trafficker to be a controlled drug. That is only sensible to me.
It would be a straight misrepresentation.

I realize that this is perhaps a bit out of order, although I think there is a connection and we have made reference to it previously. In the schedule to Bill No. C-100 there are some 90 substances which I understand fall into a prohibited class and are classified as narcotics. Can the minister tell us how many of these are not addictive?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am afraid that I cannot get into a detailed discussion of Bill No. C-100. That is another bill. In the schedule to Bill C-99 we have three drugs which we are now calling controlled drugs for the purposes of this bill. There are these three, as I have indicated. Incidentally, I presume we would be coming to that section of the bill later on. However, there are these three particular drugs and the salts and derivatives of them. For instance, I have a list of several things that might be considered to be in the barbiturate group. There is verinol, nytol, luminol.
Are they in the narcotic drug act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: No; these are barbiturates.
The hon. member for Skeena is asking about those 100 substances that are in the narcotic drug act and that might be in the category of marijuana.
Or having the same effect; that is, being classified as non-addictive.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am told that under Bill C-100, to provide for the control of the narcotic drug act these are synthetic drugs which can only be named as such. The three in the schedule to Bill No. C-99 have many derivatives and salts from these family groups. As I say, there are many trade names which different companies call them in the barbiturate group. Different companies call their products by different names. Ciba has a product in the barbiturate group. There is nembutal for Abbott Laboratories, seconal for Eli Lilly and Company, and so on. These are trade names primarily. There are only these three family groups and then there are the salts and derivatives.

Perhaps I should ask the question again. How many of the approximately 90 drugs-and I use the round figure- listed in the schedule to Bill No. C-100 are of the type of drugs that fall into the same

Food and Drugs Act
class as marijuana which I said was nonaddictive and as to which, as the minister said, "yes, even though it is non-addictive it is internationally known"? How many of these are considered to be non-addictive type of drugs similar to marijuana?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Actually I think we are quite out of order because we are discussing another bill. However, I should like to point out that all the items on the schedule to Bill No. C-100 are under international control or jurisdiction.

Shall
section 32 carry?

Before it carries may I say this. It seems strange to me-and I am thinking about the argument of the minister- that it is not necessary to engage in or establish any treatment facilities and the like because these controlled drugs under Bill No. C-99 are not considered to be as serious, yet they are serious enough that we are thinking in terms of a 10 year sentence plus a fine and on failure to pay the fine perhaps another five years maximum. We are therefore thinking in terms of a maximum 15 years in prison for a person trafficking in what is considered to be a drug which is not very serious. In his remarks the minister also made reference to the R.C.M.P. being worried about this matter and said that these are dangerous drugs with tragic results and so on. It seems to me that the minister's comments and expressions and the remedies sought in the bill do not equate with his argument that it is not a serious drug and (hat it is not a serious matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I presume that is a matter of opinion. I tried to explain our position on this matter earlier. We feel that we are going far enough in this bill. As I said earlier, this is the most forward looking legislation, of this type, of any country in the world to our knowledge. We think it is a step in the right direction. If, of course, as time goes on, we find that further steps must be taken we shall be very happy to consider them.

I have listened to this discussion between the hon. member for Skeena and the Minister of National Health and Welfare with sympathetic interest. From the point of view of logic, I think that what has been said by the hon. member for Skeena is incontestable. It may be that the minister has not fully understood the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Skeena and on that account there has been this malentente. Perhaps the misunderstanding is not only on the side of the minister, because the minister has something on his side
[Mr. Howard.)
in that these treatment centres for addicts have not been proven to be wholly without their defects.
It is not my assumption.

No, I said that the assumption that they have proven to be fully successful is quite erroneous. They are still very much in the experimental stage. The difficulties that attend the administration of just one-I refer to the one in Lexington- are so great, I am sure, as to have caused the greatest consideration before adopting them in this country. Yet I think adopting the technique and the experiment is well worth while because it is only by trying that one really ascertains whether or not the experiment is valuable. Undoubtedly in many instances constructive results flow. But, it would seem to me that the minister is on sound ground in this sense in saying that since there is some doubt about the all inclusive character of the experiment that is resorted to for the treatment of drug addicts, and as this is a pioneer measure, one should not be expected to do something which is not going to yield, according to the best human standards, substantial and desirable results. I think the way to answer that question would be for the minister to explain to the committee, and the answer is certainly not clear to me, what is the result of treatment in the case of an addict who suffers from the use of controlled drugs. We have a general idea of what is the result in terms of effect in the case of those who suffer from the use of drugs. But what kind of treatment can be provided to a person who is a victim of a barbiturate? Is it not something which is in control of the physician? Is it not something that has the same deep habit formation quality? If the minister can give us some definite information in this regard, I think he might go a long way in meeting the concern of the hon. member for Skeena. Since this is a technical problem, I hope the minister will not misunderstand me if I say I wonder why he does not have sitting at the table in front of him in addition to eminent counsel, those in his department who have special technical knowledge in this matter.

Before the minister answers perhaps I might supplement some of the observations which have been made by the hon. member for Essex East. On quickly looking over the bill, there appears to be no provision regarding a person who is a barbiturate user and there does not appear to be any consideration given to whether or not a person engaged in trafficking is also a user. The situation often arises in narcotic trafficking where a person doing the trafficking is himself

a user. I was concerned as to whether this indicates a view that barbiturate addiction is not too serious a practice. In the new measure to control narcotic drugs provision is made for treatment and I think we have for the first time recognized the problem involved in the use of narcotics. Even under the old act, as I understand it, the key question was whether a person was in possession of drugs or trafficking in them. There was nothing wrong with being a person who used a particular drug. I was wondering if the minister could comment on this point.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I am very happy to comment on all these things to the extent to which I am capable of doing so. I might mention however, with all due respect, that I think you are being lenient, Mr. Chairman, in that we seem to be discussing Bill No. C-100 every bit as much as Bill No. C-99. In this bill we are dealing with traffickers or those found in possession for the purpose of trafficking in controlled drugs.
I am happy to try to answer some of the questions which have been put to me such as those concerning the treatment of barbiturate addicts. We are informed-indeed, we are convinced-that withdrawal from any addiction there may be to those controlled drugs is not as difficult as is withdrawal, for example, from addiction to heroin. We do not feel that these controlled drugs have the same habit forming quality as narcotics. Frankly, in this present legislation we are after the trafficker; we are not legislating against those found in possession at all, except traffickers. It may develop that there is some loophole in this measure, but I should like to reiterate the statement I made earlier, twice, I think, this evening, to the effect that we feel this is the most forward looking legislation of any country in the world in this particular field. It is the first time to our knowledge that this step has been taken in any country. We feel that we are taking the correct step. We do not feel that treatment at the moment is as necessary as it is under the narcotics legislation. This is not a treatment measure. We are simply after those who traffic in these particular controlled drugs.

I am sure the minister is well intentioned but evidently he has not travelled "the main" where the flotsam and jetsam of the world can be found.
I have here a copy of the Montreal Star dated May 13, 1961. The heading reads: "Child Court Judge Says Ban 'Main' ". It reads in part:
"I hope the city passes an ordinance forbidding children from frequenting the Main," Judge
Food and Drugs Act
Penverne said yesterday as he sent Eugene Servant, 47, to penitentiary for selling goof balls to a child.
Everyone knows that in Montreal anybody, man, woman or child can go on the Main and purchase goof balls at practically every door. I have a clipping here from the Montreal Star of Saturday, April 22 headed: "Criminal Code Changes Sought-City Acts to Stem Goof Ball Scourge". Here is one from the same paper of March 28: "Warning Given Youth Centre-Goof Ball Menace Stressed". The report goes on to stress the growing menace of the goof ball. Here is another item from the Montreal Star of Friday, March 10, 1961: "Dr. Roussel Reports, 'Goof Balls' Blamed for Sharp Increase in Violent Crimes". Again, in the Gazette of Tuesday, February 14 we read: "Goof Balls -New and Tougher Laws Believed to be Answer". And in the Gazette of Wednesday, February 15 there is another headline: "Trafficking Reduced but not Eliminated-Fulton".
Fulton?

Yes, sir. -"Trafficking Reduced but not Eliminated-Fulton". It reads:
Traffic in "goof balls" (barbiturate and amphetamine drugs) at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary is reduced but not yet eliminated, justice minister E. Davie Fulton said yesterday.
These things have been the subject of traffic in the penitentiaries everywhere, and they can be obtained at practically every doorway on the Main.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: This is exactly what we are trying to cure.

I know, but you are not going about it in the right way. Possibly the hon. gentleman has made a good beginning, but I am trying to explain that traffic in these things is so widespread in Montreal that today anyone can continue trafficking in these drugs without much risk of being caught. This is from the Montreal Star of March 4, 1961:	"Enlightened Action on Goof Ball
Menace Needed". Here is an article which appeared in the Montreal Star on Wednesday, February 28 entitled "Bribes, Goof Balls and the Law". Another, which appeared in the Gazette on February 14 is entitled: "The 'Goof Ball' Menace". Again in the Gazette of April 7, is a further article called: "Those who Peddle Goof Balls". These are all editorials.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I have read most of them.
Another, from the Gazette of May 25 is headed: "Narcotic Laws and 'Goof Balls'." I have a stack several feet high upstairs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
So have I.

Food and Drugs Act

The newspapers, as is obvious from what I have been reading, consider this problem to present a real menace, but we are not being sincere in our approach. I am alarmed when I draw the attention of the committee to this. I have been telling this house about it for three years but only now is action being taken, and it is action which is mild in character. This involves the contamination of our youth, yet we are only taking mild measures to deal with it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
I think I must say a few words on the observations to which we have just listened. The hon. member claims the action we are taking is not sufficiently severe. At the moment the penalty for trafficking in narcotics is, I believe, 14 years. This legislation provides a penalty of ten years for trafficking in controlled drugs. I think that is a serious penalty, myself. This bill is designed to prevent precisely the type of thing to which the hon. member has been calling attention. It implements the recommendations of the citizens' committee. Incidentally, the hon. member indicated that I had probably heard from the mayor of Montreal about the meeting of that committee. No delegation has approached me so far. I am not sure whether or not any other member of the government has been approached but I have had no word from the citizens' committee of Montreal concerning this matter. I have the report, and I may say that practically all its recommendations have been implemented in this present bill.
(Translation):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had not intended participating in this debate because I am not of the medical profession, nor am I a druggist. However, I followed every remark made in this chamber on the subject of goof balls such as those of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque). He talked about goof balls for 30 minutes and-
And rightly so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I will tell you in a moment if he was so right. The hon. member talked on that matter for 30 minutes-
Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: -then, he made another speech during the examination of the estimates of the Minister of Justice, when he kept the floor on the same subject for another fifteen minutes. Nobody in this house would deny the nefarious effects of goof balls in the province of Quebec.
Are there goof balls in the constituency of Gaspe?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
No. Come over to Gaspe, and you will find that I have no need to fight the use of goof balls, because there are none. However, there are some in your constituency.
Mr. Chairman, I have been listening closely to my colleagues, and I wonder whether we are not a bit responsible for the situation. While we all recognize that goof balls have caused great harm to our young people, I wonder whether the way to settle the problem is to publicize this drug and to suggest all kinds of recipes to our young people.
Really, Mr. Chairman, instead of teaching bad things to our young people, we in this house who all recognize that goof balls are bad for them should try to remedy the situation; however, I do not think that can be achieved by indulging in petty politics.
Mr. Chairman, we have actually provided recipes to our young people. We have discussed goof balls, we have discussed aspirins and coca-cola, and now I am wondering whether in fact we should not have awaited the bill which was introduced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith)-
There would never have been a bill if we had stopped discussing the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
-who, I am sure, will apply the appropriate remedy to the situation.
Mr. Chairman, as I was saying a moment ago, I wish to discuss this bill not as a doctor or as a pharmacist, but I think I am entitled to discuss it as a former teacher who has always aimed at inculcating to our youth ideas that would be beneficial to the nation as a whole.
Therefore, I repeat, Mr. Chairman, this is not the place to say too much about goof balls. Anyhow, it is certainly not here that one should get the recipe for them.
We are here, on the contrary, to remedy the situation and to protect our young people.
(Text):

The hon. member would like to fiddle, like Nero, while Rome burns. He wants to be like an ostrich with his head in the sand while the storm is raging.
The minister said a moment ago that he had not received anything from Montreal regarding this subject. I should just like to quote from an editorial which appeared-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not say that I had not received anything from Montreal. I said I had not received a request in this regard from the mayor of Montreal.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to inform the hon. minister, in that event, what the recommendation is which is put forward by the mayor of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have the report here in front of me.

In view of what the minister said a moment ago, I should like to read a few lines appearing in an editorial in La Presse of Saturday, April 22, 1961, which are as follows:
(Translation):
War on barbiturates.
The report of the subcommittee which was set up by Montreal's executive committee and which is headed by the mayor-
The report reads as follows:

(f) deprive a person charged with a criminal offence of the right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty according to law in a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal,-

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say only a few words to support the important point which has been raised by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin).
The hon. member has repeated the well known legal saying that a man is innocent until he is proven guilty. I should like to add to the point that has been made.

It is up to the crown to make a case and if it does not succeed, the judge must dismiss the charge without the accused having to appear on the witness stand.
That, I feel, is one of the most important points. Under section 33, the accused has to take the stand to dismiss the presumption of guilt which hangs over his head.

I am thinking specifically of the indictment of receiving and concealing where the crown must establish possession of goods recently stolen, and then the accused has to establish that he was innocent of such possession.

Subsection 1 points out that if the accused does not plead guilty-that is the controlling situation-then the trial proceeds as if the issue to be determined were whether or not the accused was in possession of a controlled drug. Now, these are the governing words. Once the accused fails to plead guilty, then the trial proceeds as if the only issue were whether or not the accused was in possession

of a controlled drug. This provision is a clear violation of the bill of rights because it imposes a presumption of guilt, which is contrary to the bill of rights.

If the hon. member will just listen to the rest of my argument, I would point out that the controlling provision is subsection 1 of section 33. If the accused refuses to plead guilty, then the issue to be tried is whether or not he was in possession or is in possession of controlled drugs. Only when he can satisfy the court that he was not in possession of a controlled drug will he be regarded as not having come within the mischief of this section. Now, if that is not imposing upon the accused an onus which normally resides with the crown, then I will be very greatly surprised. This is done in an indirect way, and that makes the situation all the more serious because it is only by a careful reading of the provision that one sees there is no doubt that the presumption of establishing his innocence when he refuses to plead guilty is imposed upon the accused. speechtext: I should like to get some information in connection with this clause. This clause does two things. Mr. Chairman, I think I explained that quite fully both at the resolution stage and in discussion on the bill during second reading. This legislation is what is termed "roll-back legislation", and is provided to make sure that the reduction of 7 per cent in freight rates, resulting from the roll-back from 17 per cent to 10 per cent, will be covered. For that purpose, an amount of $20 million is set aside to pay the railways, through the Minister of Finance, on the order of the board of transport commissioners. The railways send their bills to the board of transport commissioners at the end of each month for the recommendation of that board, in order that the Minister of Finance can make payment. It will be recalled that last year, when a similar bill was presented to the house by my predecessor, at the same time he announced the creation of the royal commission

Freight Rates Reduction Act on transportation, he indicated that while the royal commission was making a complete study in respect of the problems of transportation in Canada, this act should be extended for another year so as to eliminate the possibility of any discrimination occurring to shippers during that period. The report of the MacPherson commission was received by the government very recently, and until legislation based on this report can be implemented in the house the government felt that this roll-back legislation should carry on for another period. Actually, all that this legislation does is to carry on the roll-back legislation which was introduced in the house two years ago.
When the government brings forward legislation based on the MacPherson report it will then consider whether or not it will carry on with this program. The provision is for one year which actually ends on April 30, 1962.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill has been considered very carefully in the Veterans Affairs Committee. Many items were discussed in the committee which I think settled some of the problems that were raised in the house when the bill was before us on an earlier occasion. A request had been made to extend the provisions of the fund to Newfoundland veterans but that was dealt with in the committee by pointing out that those who contributed to this fund were the only ones who were entitled to share in the fund.
The fund arose as a result of various activities of the Canadian army in the second world war and it is those veterans of that particular army who are entitled to the benefits of the fund. R.C.A.F. veterans, for example, cannot make use of this fund. Neither can navy veterans use the fund nor army veterans of the first world war. As I pointed out when this matter was before the house on a former occasion, the moneys in the fund were derived from the regimental funds of army units, from auxiliary services, from Bronco, from the navy, army and air force institutes and from various miscellaneous sources, all of which funds resulted, as I have mentioned, from the sale of comforts and so on to the soldiers of the Canadian army.
There are certain Canadian funds in existence from the first world war. To my knowledge only three are left now, those in Ontario, Manitoba and New Brunswick. Originally such funds existed, I believe, in nearly every province in the country but as the moneys in these funds were used up the administrations closed their doors and the funds ceased to exist.
There is still a good deal of money left in the fund we are considering now and the purpose of the bill is explained fairly adequately in the explanatory notes accompanying the bill. Without going into a clause by clause discussion of the bill at the moment, I might point out that it has been thought that the interest rates should be increased as set forth in the bill to bring them in line with interest rates paid on similar funds held by the government of Canada.
Second, the purpose of the bill is to make an adjustment in the way the salary of the secretary is fixed in order that this matter may be removed from the statute and the
Army Benevolent Fund Act salary fixed by the board itself. I understand the secretary has not received any increase in salary for a number of years and it is thought that to have his salary made statutory is not a convenient way to deal with it.
In the standing committee it was suggested by the Canadian Legion that the interest rates should be increased still further than is set forth in the bill. When you increase interest rates on this or any other fund, I suppose it is always possible to suggest that the rate should be increased still further but the figure that has been selected in this case has been chosen on the basis of the principles which have existed for the setting of the interest rate on this fund in times past, particularly in 1952 and also in 1947 when the fund was originally established. Therefore I think we had better stick to the original principles for the setting of these interest rates, and the activities of the fund, will, of course, be tailored in accordance with the amount of money available.
I think that is all I can usefully say at the present time. As I mentioned, the bill was discussed very thoroughly in the standing committee and we are bringing it forward now for consideration in committee of the whole house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I want to bring into focus the question of the interest rate payable on the fund. I think there are two courses open. One is for the fund administered by the army benevolent fund committee to be invested by them. The other is that the government should pay the same rate of interest on the fund that they paid to borrow money in the conversion loan which falls due in 1983. At the present time the prevailing rate of yield on conversion loan bonds is 5.14 per cent. If these moneys were invested at 5.14 per cent the fund would be able to carry on, as was originally planned when the act was passed in 1947, for a period of 50 years at which time the fund would be exhausted.
The Canadian Legion made the following recommendations before the veterans affairs committee:
The Canadian Legion, therefore, believes the government must accept that the minimum rate at which money can be obtained in the open market is somewhere between 4J per cent and 5 per cent, and that this should be acknowledged by establishing a rate such as 41 per cent as the minimum to be paid by the receiver general to the army benevolent fund in respect of the balance which is available to the government at all times. We believe that by increasing the rate to 41 per cent per annum it would mean that the fund would have available more adequate means with which to meet the original intent of this legislation.
There is no doubt about it, Mr. Chairman. If the 4J per cent rate were to prevail across the board in relation to these moneys, there would be a considerable increase in the return on the moneys but it would not be adequate to take care of this fund for the full period of 50 years. I am suggesting, therefore, that the yield that should be obtained from this army benevolent fund should be the same as that obtained from the conversion bonds which are yielding about 5.14 per cent. These were the last figures I had, and they may have changed fractionally since then.
Let us look at the remarks of Mr. Chad-derton, as they are recorded on page 314 of the evidence of the veterans affairs committee. He had this to say:

We started with $9,200,000. Today we have left $6,500,000. So we have spent in cold cash from the fund, we have depleted the fund, in other words, in the amount of $2,700,000. In addition, we have had revenue through interest of $3,500,000. So the total amount now spent is $6,200,000. We operate this fund on an actuarial plan, which envisaged 30 years of full operation from 1947. The act states that we must remain in business for 50 years. The actuarial plan provides for a full period of operation of 30 years with a small residue to take care of the remaining 20 years. This, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, offers a very serious problem to the army benevolent fund. I have already noted that we have left today only $6,500,000, but in accordance with this actuarial plan, we should have $7 million. So we have had to overspend to the tune of $500,000.
We had a new actuarial plan drafted at the end of the last fiscal year. The figures which the department of insurance gave us were such that we would have to reduce our expenditure for welfare grants and administration to $450,000 a year. Even with the proposed increase in interest in the bill before the parliamentary committee today, we can increase our expenditure to only $470,000 a year, even if we should get this increase in interest. The actual expenditures have averaged over the past 10 years $530,000 a year. We are facing a very serious problem, and our board sees one of two alternatives; either they must cut down on the amount that we spend each year and leave deserving cases out in the cold, or secondly, we must reduce the remaining 17 years of operation of the fund. Our board would not wish to do either of these things, because we have operated from the start on the principle that the veteran who is in trouble today is just as much entitled to assistance as the veteran who was in trouble at the start of the fund. And by the same token, if a veteran is in trouble 17 years from now, he should still have the availability of the army benevolent fund.
I asked Mr. Chadderton the following question as recorded on page 319 of the evidence:
Let me ask you another question: Do you feel that a higher rate of interest could be obtained if this fund were placed in the hands of a committee of the army benevolent fund, and that they should be allowed to invest this fund as they saw fit? You recall that it is not government money. You have already stated it. This money belongs to the veterans. Would it not be advisable to transfer to that committee from the government, or the receiver general, or the consolidated revenue fund, or whoever does the investing of the army benevolent fund?

speechtext:
I should like to thank both of the hon. members for the contributions they have made to the discussion on this matter. I might say that serious consideration was given to the views that they and other hon. members expressed in the committee and also to the views of the Canadian Legion with regard to this matter of interest rates. The arguments that were advanced then and have been advanced here are, of course, the same arguments that could have been advanced in 1947 or 1952 when this bill was originally introduced and then amended. On those occasions it is always possible, just as it is possible now, to pick out a type of security and say that this security yields a higher rate than does the security on which interest is being paid by the government under this legislation. However, after the most careful consideration of the point raised it was thought that we should

Army Benevolent Fund Act stick to the original principle which was involved in the setting of the rates of this fund so that continuity could be carried on. That is not the only reason, of course. But the rates as set bear a relation to rates on funds held by the government from other sources and on which the government pays interest rates. I think perhaps it might be useful to recall to the members of this committee that this fund came first, and then the uses of this fund came second. It was not the other way around. When this fund was originally set up, a plan for assisting veterans was not envisaged and then money supplied for that purpose. It happened in a contrary way. The fund existed, drawn from the sources that I have already referred to; and because those funds existed, it was then determined that those funds should be used for the purposes developed by the army benevolent fund.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask a question? Who determined how this money should be spent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext: It was determined by parliament in 1947. It was determined by the parliament of Canada, by this House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext: Not by the veterans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
The purposes are quite similar to the purposes of the R.C.A.F. benevolent fund and of the navy fund also. The purposes came second; the fund came first.
Again I thank hon. members for their contributions both in committee and here to the discussion of this matter. However, I wish to assure them that, after very careful consideration, we feel that a fair and equitable rate of interest is one that is based on the policy which has been carried forward from the time of the inception of the army benevolent fund. Accordingly, I hope the increase which is recommended by the bill will receive the support of the members of the House of Commons.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I must say that I am particularly disappointed that the government has not seen fit to accede to the recommendation and suggestion made by the Canadian Legion. This money does not belong to the government. It is money that has been provided by the veterans over a period of time and for particular purposes. It has been provided for the aid which this fund can give to veterans. Because the money is not government money and because it is being held by the
government, it seems to me that the government should give to this fund an interest rate which would normally be given to money which is borrowed by the government.
I think the suggestion made by the Canadian Legion was a reasonable one. At this particular time when the fund is having just a little bit of trouble in following the actuarial plan which was set up for it, I feel that this is one way of helping the fund to carry on with the good work being done. I feel that this recommendation should have been accepted. I agreed wholeheartedly with the recommendation in committee; and even at this late stage I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that maybe it is not too late to give some active and favourable consideration to this suggestion.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF INTEREST, PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES, ETC.
speechtext: Carried.

speechtext: May I inquire what legislation, if any, will be discussed tomorrow and what the estimates are for the rest of the week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will take third reading of Bill No. C-77, dealing with agricultural development and then second reading of the bill dealing with the War Veterans Allowance Act, which bill will be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. Then I think perhaps we should finish the matter we were debating tonight, namely Bill No. C-88, to amend the Army Benevolent Fund Act. After those items are completed, we will then take up the estimates of the Secretary of State. For Thursday, Friday and Saturday I have already announced the departments that we shall be considering. On Thursday we start, by arrangement, with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. Then, if we have not finished with the estimates of the Secretary of State tomorrow, I would suggest that we take the estimates of the Secretary of State after those of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. The third one will be fisheries and then will come public works.
